articles.title: Top Kennedy Center official urged closure due to financial problems, not poor conditions, lawyers argue
articles.summary: Eighteen months after President Donald Trump stepped in to remake the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in his image, a top official worried abo...
articles.body:
Eighteen months after President Donald Trump stepped in to remake the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts in his image, a top official worried about the Washington institution's hemorrhaging finances urged for it to be shut down, according to court documents filed on behalf of the Ohio congresswoman seeking to stop the center from being shuttered.

"She told him we need to get shut and need a unanimous vote," reads a series of September text messages describing a conversation between the board of trustees Vice Chair Jennifer Fischer and Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick, who has been a driving force in the Trump administration's efforts to renovate the Kennedy Center by, among other things, placing the president's name on the building. "She said we are broke and borrowed money to pay the bills."

The tranche of documents filed Friday night on behalf of Rep. Joyce Beatty, an ex-officio board member, seek to undermine the Trump administration's contention that the $200 million renovation it is pursuing is due to "dangerously dilapidated and decrepit" conditions that require it to be shuttered for two years.

The Kennedy Center referred CNN to the Department of Justice for questions about the filing. CNN has reached out to the DOJ.

A judge in the case has issued a temporary restraining order compelling the center to remain operating while the lawsuit continues, which Kennedy Center officials have done by continuing programming inside a portion of the campus known as the REACH. The Trump administration is seeking to have the judge's order lifted.

Lawyers for Beatty argued in the Friday filing that she and other trustees never saw an analysis by a contractor that contradicts the case for closing the center for two years over pursuing the renovations in phases. Instead, the lawyers say in a news release accompanying the filing, Trump and his managers appeared to have hidden that information from the board.

According to Beatty's attorneys, Kennedy Center Director Matt Floca insisted to the venue's trustees that construction costs would double if the center took a phased approach. He based that assessment on a contractor's report that used a preliminary estimate of the cost difference. But a revised estimate that was never seen by the board before it approved the building's closure put that extra cost closer to $41 million, according to the filing.

"The record now confirms that they knew that estimate was wrong," the attorneys said in the filing about Kennedy Center officials.

Center officials also contended that $257 million appropriated by Congress for the center's renovations has to be spent by the end of the 2029 fiscal year, when in reality they have until the 2034 fiscal year to spend the money, Beatty's attorneys argued.

"The court told this Board to do its job. As a trustee, I have a duty to be accountable. Yet Trump and his handpicked management failed to follow the law, hid facts that didn't fit their narrative, and rubberstamped Trump's wishes," Beatty said in the news release. "I have a duty to protect this living memorial to President Kennedy on behalf of the American people. I will keep fighting to do my job, make sure the law is followed, and ensure that Trump cannot tear down the Kennedy Center to satisfy his ego."

CNN previously reported that the legal saga and wave of cancellations from performers that ensued since Trump became board chairman presented financial challenges for the institution. With the center's future in limbo, the cultural institution moved the annual Kennedy Center Honors to the Capitol One Arena in downtown DC.

articles.title: Traders pour nearly $1.3 billion into predicting who will control Congress
articles.summary: Kalshi says nearly $1.3 billion has been traded on midterm elections markets, surpassing 2024 presidential election volume as bettors size up key races.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: More than $1.2 billion has now been traded on Kalshi’s midterm markets for the 2026 election, surpassing the platform’s volume during the 2024 presidential election year, according to data shared exclusively with Fox News Digital. The surge stands out in a midterm year, when there's no presidential race to draw the same level of national attention. Unlike traditional polls, which capture voter sentiment at a particular moment, prediction markets shift as traders react to debates, fundraising, endorsements and breaking news, offering campaigns and political observers a real-time read on how expectations are changing. THE BATTLE FOR CONGRESS GETS A WALL STREET-STYLE SCOREBOARD POWERED BY REAL MONEY The money is flowing into a contest that could determine whether President Donald Trump faces a Congress ready to advance his agenda or one ready to instead launch back-to-back investigations into his administration. Kalshi traders are wagering on individual House, Senate and gubernatorial races, as well as which party will control each chamber come January 2027. The company’s industry data, obtained by Fox News Digital, offers a glimpse of how traders are sizing up the election and where their predictions diverge. The data also shows a sharp difference in how traders inside and outside two states are betting on closely watched Senate races. In Maine, out-of-state traders are putting more money on Democrat Troy Jackson than in-state traders are: 61% versus 36%. In Michigan, 65% of out-of-state traders’ money is on Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, compared with 49% of in-state traders’ money. That means traders in both states are putting less money on the Democratic candidate than traders elsewhere are. Kalshi launched its Midterms Hub in July, combining live market odds with polling averages, fundraising data, historical election results and political news for House, Senate and gubernatorial races. Law enforcement traders put 67.9% of their dollars on Republicans, the biggest GOP lean among the listed industries. Meanwhile, arts and entertainment traders showed the strongest Democratic tilt, putting 60.1% of their money on Democrats. The divide also appears in other fields. Traders in mining, energy and chemicals put 62.6% of their dollars on Republicans, while education traders put 58.3% on Democrats. However, in legal services and electronics, traders were nearly split. PREDICTION MARKETS FAVOR DEMOCRATS IN NEW YORK, NEW JERSEY, VIRGINIA ELECTION DAY RACES CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The figures show where traders expect the races to land, not which party they personally support or how workers in those industries plan to vote. With control of Congress on the line, Kalshi’s markets will keep shifting as traders react to new developments in the closing weeks of the midterm campaigns.

articles.title: Comer says there’s a ‘big possibility’ Peltola won’t be seated if she wins
articles.summary: Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) said Sunday there is a “big possibility” that former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) won’t be seated even if she wins Alaska’s Senate r...
articles.body:
Rep. James Comer (R-Ky.) said Sunday there is a "big possibility" that former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) won't be seated even if she wins Alaska's Senate race, following reports that her campaign participated in a " ballot-stacking " scheme.

Comer, who chairs the House Oversight Committee, was asked during his appearance on Fox News's "Sunday Morning" if there was a possibility Peltola would not be seated even if she won the election.

"That's a big possibility. I have not spoken to Sen. Thune about that," Comer said, referring to Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.).

"We kind of tend to operate within the confinement of the House with respect to our investigations, but at the end of the day, I think the American people can see loud and clear what was done here," the congressman continued.

Comer, particularly, has heavily criticized Peltola's campaign over a New York Times report that alleged her campaign and national Democrats recruited another candidate who shared the same name as her Republican opponent, incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan, in order to dilute the GOP vote.

"Ballot-stacking" is a common practice, especially in Alaska's unusual nonpartisan, top four voting system. GOP strategists previously told The Hill that it is not illegal.

"We cannot allow this to happen. And the fact that there are a lot of people involved in the Democrat National Party who have been silent on this, and the question remains: Who all was involved? When did this involvement begin? Did money change hands? That's a big question," Comer said Sunday. "That's probably the biggest question that needs to be answered. Did money change hands? And then you know what laws were broken after that?"

He has already launched a probe into Peltola's involvement in the operation — scheduling transcribed, in-person interviews for both former Peltola campaign manager Elisa Rios and Democratic operative Jerid Kurtz.

Comer requested that Rios testify on Nov. 5 and Kurtz on Nov. 6.

Sullivan said earlier Sunday that he would accept the election results even if he lost, though Sen. Tim Scott (R-S.C.) dodged answering the same question.

articles.title: Chuva provoca deslizamentos e erosão em rodovia de Santa Isabel | G1
articles.standfirst: Temporal deste domingo (1º) também causou alagamentos em vários pontos da cidade e derrubou o muro de uma casa.
articles.summary: Temporal deste domingo (1º) também causou alagamentos em vários pontos da cidade e derrubou o muro de uma casa.
articles.body:
A chuva forte deste domingo (1º) provocou deslizamentos de terra, alagamentos e erosão em Santa Isabel . O temporal também causou o desmoronamento do muro de uma casa. As ocorrências foram registradas em diferentes pontos do município.

Segundo a Defesa Civil de Santa Isabel, uma erosão foi identificada na Rodovia Arthur Matheus, cerca de 500 metros após a entrada do Portal, no sentido da Rodovia Presidente Dutra. O problema atingiu parte do acostamento e comprometeu a borda do pavimento, próximo à defensa metálica.

O Departamento de Estradas de Rodagem (DER) foi acionado para avaliar a situação e tomar as providências necessárias.

Na Estrada do Monte Negro, na altura da Vila Alpina, um deslizamento de terra bloqueou parcialmente a via. Outro deslizamento foi identificado na Rua Japão.

Durante o atendimento, a Defesa Civil não identificou riscos aos moradores. A equipe deve retornar ao local nesta segunda-feira (2) para continuar a avaliação.

O muro de uma casa desmoronou na Rua Hiroshima. Segundo a Defesa Civil, as chuvas intensas podem ter contribuído para o ocorrido. O morador também relatou um possível vazamento de água em uma viela próxima.

Os alagamentos foram registrados nos seguintes locais:

Avenida Coronel Bertoldo, no sentido da Rodovia Presidente Dutra;

Avenida Manoel Ferraz de Campos Salles, no cruzamento com a Rua Santa Cruz;

Rua Washington Luiz, no cruzamento com a Rua João Pio Ferraz.

A Defesa Civil alerta que as chuvas dos últimos dias e a previsão de novas precipitações exigem atenção, principalmente em áreas de encostas e locais com histórico de deslizamentos. O aumento da umidade do solo pode favorecer novos deslizamentos de terra.

Segundo a Defesa Civil, novembro começou com registros de chuva e ocorrências no município, após um outubro marcado por precipitações expressivas.

Até 18 de outubro, o acumulado de chuva em Santa Isabel havia chegado a aproximadamente 215 milímetros, de acordo com um levantamento do órgão.

A previsão para esta segunda-feira (2) é de novas pancadas de chuva, com rajadas de vento e descargas elétricas.

O Instituto Nacional de Meteorologia (Inmet) emitiu um alerta amarelo de tempestades. A previsão é de chuva entre 20 e 30 milímetros por hora, podendo chegar a 50 milímetros por dia, ventos de 40 a 60 km/h e possibilidade de granizo.

Modelos meteorológicos indicam acumulado de aproximadamente 25 milímetros de chuva na região nesta segunda-feira (2).

A Defesa Civil de Santa Isabel orienta os moradores a redobrar os cuidados durante a chuva. A recomendação é evitar atravessar ruas alagadas, passar por locais com enxurradas ou permanecer perto de encostas com sinais de instabilidade.

“É importante observar o surgimento de rachaduras no solo, muros e paredes, inclinação de árvores ou postes, movimentação de terra e aparecimento anormal de água em barrancos.”

Ao identificar qualquer sinal de risco, a recomendação é se afastar do local e comunicar imediatamente os órgãos de emergência.

Rodovia Arthur Matheus, em Santa Isabel, teve erosão com solapamento de trecho do acostamento e comprometimento da borda do pavimento, junto à defensa metálica — Foto: Defesa Civil de Santa Isabel/Divulgação

articles.title: Atendimento humano no SAC: novas regras começam a valer hoje | G1
articles.standfirst: Mudança foi prevista em decreto publicado em outubro. Exigência de manutenção de atendimento humano por chat ou telefone vale para todos os dias, entre as 8h e as 20h.
articles.summary: O novo decreto para SACs exige que bancos, operadoras e aéreas garantam contato com atendentes humanos por chat ou telefone todos os dias da semana.
articles.body:
Começam a valer nesta segunda-feira (2) as mudanças nas regras de funcionamento dos serviços de atendimento aos consumidores, os SACs, mantidos por empresas. A principal alteração é a exigência de atendimento humano, todos os dias, entre as 8h e as 20h .

O decreto do governo federal com as mudanças foi publicado em 13 de outubro , com prazo de 20 dias para começar a valer.

As medidas são apenas para empresas cujos serviços são regulados pelo governo. Entram nessa categoria operadoras de telefonia e de planos de saúde, empresas aéreas, concessionárias de energia e empresas do setor financeiro, como bancos e fintechs .

O decreto também determina que empresas de transporte individual ou de encomendas, como a Uber, cujos serviços não são regulados, prestem informações ao governo sobre o atendimento aos consumidores.

A principal medida é a que garante que os consumidores consigam ser atendidos por um humano, entre as 8h e as 20h, todos os dias, em canais eletrônicos, como os chats, e por ligação telefônica .

De acordo com o governo, essa exigência corrige uma flexibilização nas regras dos SACs feita durante a pandemia, que permitiu a ampliação do uso de ferramentas digitais e reduziu o atendimento feito por pessoas.

O decreto diz que as empresas deverão assegurar aos consumidores o acesso imediato à opção de cancelamento dos contratos e ao atendimento por humano, seja nos canais digitais ou nas chamadas telefônicas.

E que não poderão utilizar mais que cinco níveis de atendimento para finalizar a demanda dos consumidores.

Em relação aos canais telefônicos, o texto diz que as empresas deverão retornar ao consumidor quando uma chamada for interrompida antes da conclusão do atendimento. O prazo máximo para o contato é de 300 segundos, ou seja, cinco minutos.

articles.title: Servidor suspeito de observar mulheres em banheiro é afastado | G1
articles.standfirst: A Prefeitura de Pimenteiras determinou a abertura de um Processo Administrativo Disciplinar (PAD) para apurar o caso e investigar a conduta do servidor.
articles.summary: A Prefeitura de Pimenteiras determinou a abertura de um Processo Administrativo Disciplinar (PAD) para apurar o caso e investigar a conduta do servidor.
articles.body:
O servidor de uma Unidade Básica de Saúde (UBS) de Pimenteiras, no Centro-Norte do Piauí, foi afastado das funções após ser denunciado por supostamente observar mulheres em um banheiro da unidade. A informação foi confirmada pela prefeita do município, Lúcia Lacerda.

A denúncia veio à tona após a circulação de um vídeo que mostra um homem olhando pelas frestas de uma porta. Segundo a prefeita, o caso aconteceu no dia 28 de outubro.

De acordo com o relato que acompanha as imagens, o homem seria servidor da prefeitura e estaria observando mulheres no local. No entanto, as gravações não permitem confirmar quem aparece no vídeo nem identificar o ambiente onde a cena foi registrada.

"Mandei abrir o PAD, que é o Processo Administrativo para apurar a responsabilidade e punir com o rigor da lei não vamos ficar em silêncio diante de uma situação desta natureza. Toda mulher tem que se sentir segura dentro de uma unidade de saúde. Estamos apurando com seriedade e dando todo apoio às mulheres.", disse a prefeita.

O g1 borrou a imagem do homem que aparece nas gravações para preservar sua identidade, uma vez que os fatos denunciados ainda estão sendo apurados.

Até a última atualização desta reportagem, o g1 não havia conseguido localizar a defesa do servidor.

Leia a íntegra da nota da Prefeitura de Pimenteiras

Como prefeita de Pimenteiras e Presidente do Conselho da Mulher Municipalista da APPM, venho manifestar meu profundo repúdio a qualquer atitude que represente desrespeito, constrangimento, violência ou violação da intimidade e da dignidade das mulheres.

Ao tomar conhecimento de denúncia envolvendo um servidor municipal de uma Unidade Básica de Saúde do nosso município, relacionada a uma suposta conduta de violar a intimidade de mulheres, determinei imediatamente ao Secretário Municipal de Saúde que adotasse as medidas administrativas necessárias para a abertura do Processo Administrativo Disciplinar, a fim de que os fatos sejam devidamente apurados.

articles.title: Dingell says Stevens defending Rogers endorsement was ‘painful’
articles.summary: Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) on Sunday called Rep. Haley Stevens’s (D-Mich.) interview with CNN’s Anderson Cooper, where she defended her endorsement of former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in Michigan’s Senate race, “one of the most painful interviews I’ve ever watched.” Cooper, after a tense exchange with Stevens about why she changed her mind to endorse…
articles.body:
Rep. Debbie Dingell (D-Mich.) on Sunday called Rep. Haley Stevens’s (D-Mich.) interview with CNN’s Anderson Cooper, where she defended her endorsement of former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.) in Michigan’s Senate race , “one of the most painful interviews I’ve ever watched.”

Cooper, after a tense exchange with Stevens about why she changed her mind to endorse Rogers over Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed (D), quickly apologized to Dingell for having her on right after Stevens without Dingell knowing.

“First of all, I’m going to say I’m not sure I would have done this if I had known she was going to be on immediately before me,” Dingell began. “That was one of the most painful interviews I’ve ever watched. I have been worried about her all last week. She’s a human being. I’ve had multiple conversations with her. I’m far from being the only one that has.”

Dingell said she worried this would be a “distraction” from electing Democrats who will address growing concerns over the cost of living, and that the focus on Stevens’s endorsement of Rogers left Dingell “sad.”

“And I think that this is backfiring,” she later said. “Abdul has raised more money today, more than a million dollars, talking to different people that have been at different polls. … By the end of the day, I thought Abdul was going to win, but I felt a shift just being out, as I always am, this afternoon. So I think this race is going to be close.”

Cooper asked if El-Sayed should have done anything different, as sources close to the matter said the candidate asked Stevens not to attend a campaign event at a church with him Sunday morning.

“I’m actually the one that called her and said, ‘This has become a distraction,'” Dingell said. “I don’t know what I wish. This has been a very difficult week to watch, and I know that Michigan is tired of the drama, that they’re really worried about everyday issues.”

Cooper later asked Dingell if Stevens said she would not endorse Rogers during their call Saturday night, a question the CNN anchor asked Stevens several times in their interview.

“Yes, she did,” Dingell said. “Multiple times.”

The endorsement stirred controversy, with members of Stevens’s staff resigning and Michigan Democrats fuming at the lawmaker. Other Democrats called the move a “betrayal,” with Rep. Yassamin Ansari (D-Ariz.) calling it “insane.”

“There’s a fascist dictator in the White House,” she wrote on the social platform X . “Mike Rogers is a racist who supports a nationwide abortion ban AND the fascist dictator. With this move, Haley Stevens is no longer a Democrat.”

National Republicans, including President Trump, celebrated Stevens’s endorsement . The president said he would “ love to have ” her join the GOP.

articles.title: In Alaska fishing community, the Dan Sullivan episode takes an ominous turn as FBI comes knocking
articles.summary: PETERSBURG, Alaska (AP) — In the sleepy Alaskan fishing community of Petersburg, nobody has seen Dan J. His rustic home stood dark a day after FBI agents vis...
articles.body:
PETERSBURG, Alaska (AP) — In the sleepy Alaskan fishing community of Petersburg, nobody has seen Dan J. Sullivan for weeks.

His rustic home stood dark a day after FBI agents visited friends who donated to his quixotic campaign to unseat the Republican senator with the same first and last name — Dan S. Sullivan. The only display of politics at his home was a yard sign from the League of Women Voters: "Stand Up for Democracy: Vote 2026."

What may have begun as a ploy to harm the reelection prospects of Sen. Sullivan has taken a serious turn as the Trump administration weighs criminal charges over a campaign tactic known as "ballot stacking."

"It just seems like such a waste of our taxpayer money," said Sharon Hunter, a Petersburg resident who, with her husband, donated $1,000 to Dan J. Sullivan, a former elementary school teacher. FBI agents knocked on her door Saturday during a round of interviews with the campaign's dozen contributors.

"I'm a bit incredulous about their whole angle," Hunter said, "because they're targeting a person who's been a real contributor in this community."

Recruiting candidates to draw votes away from an opponent has been a part of Alaska's quirky politics for years. This time around, the state's open primary and ranked choice voting systems add another wrinkle, making it easier for lesser-known candidates to play spoilers when no contender secures a majority.

The tactic has drawn fresh scrutiny as the incumbent Sullivan fights off a serious challenge from Democrat Mary Peltola, a former U.S. representative, in a race that could determine control of the Senate.

Peltola has denied any role in the alleged chicanery as she has sought to distance herself from a New York Times article published last week that linked a group backing the former congresswoman to a Democratic operative trying to recruit decoy candidates.

"This is Alaska. We're not in the business of tricking each other up here," Peltola told supporters at a rally in Anchorage last week.

Dan J. Sullivan's entry into the race has drawn scrutiny since June, when the Alaska Division of Elections tried to remove him from the primary ballot, determining he had not filed his candidacy as a Republican in "good faith." That finding was overturned by state courts. To avoid any confusion, state officials identify Dan S. Sullivan on the ballot as a Republican and the incumbent.

Dan J. Sullivan repeatedly said he entered the race on his own accord and had no contact with Peltola's campaign — "zero, none, zilch," he told The Associated Press in June. He answered "no" when asked if any Democratic operatives had contacted him to run.

"This is my choice," he said at the time.

A federal lawsuit brought by the Trump administration to revive efforts to undermine the former teacher's candidacy — and challenge a potential Peltola win by blocking certification of the election results — was dismissed on Sunday by a federal judge. The Justice Department quickly appealed.

AP's efforts to reach Dan J. Sullivan since The Times article have been unsuccessful. Several of the donors AP interviewed said they have not spoken to him in quite some time.

The senator, meanwhile, is seeking to ride the controversy to a third term.

"My costume is the real Dan Sullivan – not the fake guy," he quipped to trick-or-treaters Saturday night.

The controversy has thrust Petersburg, a fishing community of 3,000 known as "Little Norway" for its late 19th century settlers, into the center of a federal investigation and a crush of media attention.

It's the type of small town where everyone seems to know everyone else's business, and more than a dozen residents said they liked and admired Dan J. Sullivan, calling him a creative teacher who ran an after-school program, Little Kids Rock, to teach guitar.

At a lively Halloween party at Kito's Kave, a local dive, a patron poked fun at the surge of interest by dressing up as an FBI agent. Another wore a "Petersburg Election Scandal" prison placard around her neck. The charge: "Being a Registered Voter in Alaska."

Retired fisherman Ed Wood said he wrote a $1,000 check to Dan J. Sullivan's campaign to repay the support Sullivan and his wife gave to a costly, decade-long battle to block the state from logging a forested hillside that sits above Petersburg.

Another donor, retired boat seller Charles Flint, described Sullivan as a "liberal thinker" who sometimes voted for Republicans. Flint said that Dan J. Sullivan never told him why he entered the race.

"He probably viewed himself more as a spoiler than a legitimate long shot," said Flint, who has a "Mary for U.S. Senate" yard sign supporting the Democrat outside his coastal home. "I'm sure he's probably thinking now, 'Maybe I shouldn't have done this.'"

Friends said they are certain that Dan J. Sullivan never expected to generate so much attention, let alone from federal law enforcement.

FBI agents have descended on the town in recent days as federal authorities expanded a monthslong criminal probe into allegations that Democratic campaigners sought to recruit candidates to run against the incumbent senator. Most of Dan J.'s donors live in Petersburg and together contributed $7,150. Those questioned said the agents asked them whether they had felt deceived by the lesser-known Sullivan.

Anna Holmes and her husband contributed $500 to Dan J. Sullivan's campaign and were surprised when FBI agents showed up Friday night to question them. The agents told the couple they were investigating "campaign finance" violations, Holmes said.

They also asked the couple whether they had intended to contribute to Sen. Sullivan's campaign.

"I told the agent I would not have done that," said Holmes.

Not everyone in Petersburg defended Sullivan.

Amanda Ohmer said she was shocked when her son's former teacher entered the Senate race in May as a Republican, three days after Peltola visited Petersburg on a campaign stop. Ohmer said she believed he was a well-known liberal and attended an anti-Trump protest in town.

"You don't see a Republican at a No Kings protest," said Ohmer, a bartender at the local Moose Lodge.

She said she supported the federal investigation and is irked by friends who've rallied around Dan J. Sullivan.

"It's sleazy," said Ohmer. "Just because Republicans do it, too, doesn't make it right."

Electoral dirty tricks such as promoting so-called decoy candidates are not uncommon in Alaska, a state with a history of tight races. About 60% of 600,000 registered voters identify as independents — one of the highest percentages in the country.

As recently as 2024, the Alaska Republican Party fought to keep on the ballot an imprisoned felon with no ties to the state who was running as a Democrat for the U.S. House of Representatives seat then held by Peltola.

Mustian reported from New Orleans. Associated Press writers Becky Bohrer in Juneau, Alaska, and Nicholas Riccardi in Washington contributed reporting.

articles.title: Roberto Gómez: "No puede haber un escándalo en cada partido"
articles.standfirst: El periodista analiza todo lo que ha ocurrido con los árbitros durante su conversación con Raúl Varela en La Tribu
articles.summary: El periodista critica el nivel del arbitraje español en su conversación con Raúl Varela en La Tribu
articles.body: Roberto Gómez no se mordió la lengua a la hora de analizar la actualidad arbitral del fútbol español. En su intervención en La Tribu, junto a Raúl Varela, el periodista mostró su preocupación por los últimos episodios polémicos y cuestionó que el debate se centre en las explicaciones de los colegiados en lugar de hacerlo en sus decisiones sobre el terreno de juego. "La noticia del fin de semana ha sido que hablan los árbitros. ¿Queríais que hablaran los árbitros? Pues ya hablan los árbitros. Pero el sistema está mal", comenzó señalando Roberto Gómez, que considera que el nuevo formato no aborda el verdadero problema. El periodista puso el foco también en los árbitros que trabajan en el VAR y que, a su juicio, quedan fuera del debate público: "Aquí unos hablan y otros ponen el cazo". Gómez cuestionó que se centre la atención en dos o tres colegiados mientras otros responsables de las decisiones arbitrales no ofrecen explicaciones. Raúl Varela dejó claro que no está en contra de que los árbitros hablen después de los partidos. "A mí no me molesta que hablen, lo que quiero es que piten bien, que no se produzca lo del juez de línea, que no se produzca lo del penalti", explicó el presentador. Varela fue, además, especialmente contundente al valorar lo sucedido durante el fin de semana: "Ayer fue un domingo malísimo, arbitralmente hablando". En ese sentido, Roberto Gómez lanzó una reflexión sobre la frecuencia de las polémicas: "No puede haber un escándalo en cada partido. Esto no es el nivel del arbitraje español". Gómez matizó que los árbitros pueden tener actuaciones mejores o peores y que los errores forman parte del fútbol, pero considera que la situación actual está generando demasiados focos de controversia. "Puede haber errores, árbitros que estén mejor, peor... pero no puede ser que sean noticia...", insistió. Otro de los momentos más destacados de la intervención llegó cuando Roberto Gómez amplió sus críticas a los comentaristas arbitrales que analizan las jugadas polémicas en los medios de comunicación: "Están haciendo mucho daño al arbitraje". "Hoy se trata de saber aplicar el reglamento", explicó Gómez, antes de recurrir a una comparación para reforzar su argumento: "¿Por aprenderme el Código Penal voy a ser buen abogado? Tendré que saber interpretarlo. Y los únicos que saben interpretarlo bien son los que están en el terreno de juego".

articles.title: Mamdani says Trump agrees to grant visa so mother can attend funeral of teen killed in Bronx shooting
articles.summary: Mayor Zohran Mamdani said President Donald Trump agreed to grant a visa to the mother of a 15-year-old who was fatally shot in the Bronx last week.
articles.body: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said that President Donald Trump has agreed to grant a visa to the mother of a teenage immigrant from Ghana who was shot and killed last week in the Bronx. "The murder of a child is a pain no parent should have to endure, let alone from thousands of miles away," Mamdani wrote Saturday on X. "Javits Frimpong’s mother deserves to say goodbye to her son in person. I just got off the phone with President Trump and he has agreed to grant her visa immediately." Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House for comment. TRUMP LEAVES STAGE MID-SPEECH TO EMBRACE PARENTS OF 12-YEAR-OLD KILLED BY STRAY BULLET IN THE BRONX Javits Frimpong, 15, was heading to school in a Bronx neighborhood shortly before 9:30 a.m. on Thursday when he was shot in the abdomen, according to New York City Police. He was rushed to a hospital, where he was pronounced dead. No arrests have been made in connection with the shooting. The incident remains under investigation. "All of New York City is mourning this tragedy," the mayor said. Frimpong arrived in the Bronx from Ghana a year ago to stay with his father and begin a new life in the U.S., according to U.S. Rep. Ritchie Torres, D-N.Y. TRUMP, MAMDANI SET TO MEET AGAIN ON MAYOR’S HOME TURF AFTER MONTHS OF POLITICAL WHIPLASH "Our entire borough is mourning a young man who should have had his whole future ahead of him," Torres said. "Every child in the Bronx deserves to walk to school without fearing for their life, and no parent should ever have to endure what Javits’s father, Thomas, is enduring now." Thomas Frimpong described his son as a quiet teenager. He told reporters that he learned just days before the shooting that his son was being bullied at school. "It was the principal who told me," Thomas Frimpong said. "He said two guys are disturbing my son, so he has suspended the two guys. My son is at school. He’s innocent, so I call him. I talk with my son, he said 'Dad, I’m okay.'" Ghanaian Foreign Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa said on X that Ghanaian officials in New York are coordinating with local authorities, adding that the foreign ministry "will work tirelessly with U.S. authorities to ensure justice is secured." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He also said he welcomes Mamdani's intervention and Trump’s "timely decision" to grant a visa to the victim's mother. "Madam Doris Adu Gyamfi’s pain as a loving mother is unimaginable and indeed everything must be done to ensure she is present to pay her respects," the foreign minister said. The Ghanaian government "will take care of the full cost of Madam Adu Gyamfi’s travels and also stands ready to contribute towards a dignifying funeral," he added. The Associated Press contributed to this report.

articles.title: How the president’s party has fared in every US midterm election since 1946
articles.summary: Only twice in the past 20 midterms has the president’s party gained House seats. Polls suggest 2026 won’t be the third.
articles.body:
On Tuesday, Americans head to the polls for the United States midterm elections, held halfway through a president’s four-year term. Voters will choose all 435 members of the US House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats. The voting will decide which party controls Congress for the next two years.

Although the president’s name won’t appear on the ballot, the vote is widely seen as a verdict on the presidency, and the president’s party almost always pays the price.

In 18 of the 20 midterms held from 1946 to 2022, voters took House seats away from the party in control of the White House. The average loss was 26 seats. Only Bill Clinton’s Democrats in 1998 and George W Bush’s Republicans in 2002 bucked the trend.

Political scientists call this the “presidential penalty”, or the “midterm penalty”. The president’s party tends to lose seats simply because it holds power as voters use the midterms to put a check on the White House.

The chart below shows how many House seats the president’s party has won or lost in each midterm since 1946 from Harry S Truman to Joe Biden.

Democratic presidents have suffered the biggest midterm defeats since 1946. On average, their party has lost about 29 House seats in a midterm, compared with about 23 under Republican presidents.

The largest loss came in 2010, two years after Barack Obama became the first African American elected president, when Democrats lost 64 House seats and Republicans took control of the chamber. The Democrats under Truman lost 56 seats in 1946, and under Clinton, they lost 54 in 1994, each time losing control of the House.

The worst Republican defeats came under Dwight D Eisenhower when the party lost 50 seats in 1958 and Gerald Ford when it lost 48 in 1974. Donald Trump’s first midterm in 2018 cost Republicans 42 seats and control of the House.

Big losses often cost the president’s party its majority. In seven of the 20 midterms since 1946 (1946, 1954, 1994, 2006, 2010, 2018 and 2022), the House changed hands.

The president’s party has lost Senate seats in 13 of the 20 midterms since 1946 but lost control of the chamber in only six: 1946, 1954, 1986, 1994, 2006 and 2014.

Unlike the House of Representatives, where every seat is up for election every two years, only about a third of the Senate’s 100 seats are contested in each cycle because senators serve six-year terms and their elections are staggered. That means which states are voting can matter as much as the national mood.

Eisenhower’s Republicans suffered the biggest Senate loss in the period, giving up 13 seats in 1958. Truman’s Democrats lost 12 in 1946, and Obama’s Democrats lost nine in 2014, handing control of the chamber to Republicans.

At times, the two chambers have moved in opposite directions. In 1982, Ronald Reagan’s Republicans lost 26 House seats but gained one in the Senate. In 2018, Trump’s Republicans lost the House but added a Senate seat, and in 2022, Biden’s Democrats lost the House while gaining one seat in the Senate.

These split results show that a backlash against the president does not land evenly across Congress. A party can hold its ground on a favourable Senate map while losing competitive House districts.

What does it mean to lose the House or Senate?

Losing seats and losing control are not the same thing. Lyndon Johnson’s Democrats lost 47 House seats in 1966 but kept their majority. Twenty years later, Reagan’s Republicans lost only four House seats but lost the Senate after an eight-seat setback.

Control of the chambers decides who sets the agenda and passes legislation. A bill must pass both chambers before it reaches the president for his approval or veto, so an opposition majority in either can block the president’s plans.

A House majority can also mean a party is able to launch investigations and impeach a president while a Senate majority can reject the president’s nominees, including federal judges, who serve for life.

This year, Democrats need to gain three seats to win the House and four to win the Senate. A 50-50 split in the Senate would leave Republicans in control because Vice President JD Vance may cast tie-breaking votes.

articles.title: US midterms: 1 day to go – Democrats rally around El-Sayed amid attacks
articles.summary: Democrats slam Haley Stevens over her endorsement of a Republican candidate a day before the polls.
articles.body:
With one day to go before the United States midterm elections , campaigning has reached a fever pitch with Democratic and Republican leaders pulling out all the stops to mobilise voters.

Democrats are hoping to flip control of both chambers of Congress, which is currently controlled by US President Donald Trump’s Republican Party.

All 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate’s 100 seats are up for grabs on Tuesday. Voting will also be held to elect governors in 36 of the 50 US states.

With the cost-of-living crisis, exacerbated by the US-Israel war on Iran, becoming one of the key talking points of these elections, here’s where things stand as of Monday:

What’s happened on the campaign trail in the past 24 hours?

In a dramatic political development on Sunday, Democratic Congresswoman Haley Stevens threw her support behind Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers over her own party’s nominee, Abdul El-Sayed, in Michigan – one of the most closely watched races of the US midterm elections. Stevens had lost Michigan’s Democratic Senate primary in August to El-Sayed.

Her announcement followed weeks of tension with El-Sayed over US support to Israel, which has been accused of committing genocide in Gaza. El-Sayed has opposed military support to Israel, arguing that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu pushed the US into the Iran war. Stevens has accused El-Sayed of anti-Semitism for his criticism of Israeli actions in Gaza.

El-Sayed said a vote for his rival Rogers “is going to be a vote for Donald Trump” as his campaign reportedly saw a fundraising surge after Stevens crossed party lines.

Democratic leaders have rallied behind El-Sayed, who has faced Islamophobic attacks during the campaign.

The chairman of the Democratic Party in Michigan criticised Stevens. “She does not speak for that larger community,” Curtis Hertel said in an interview with CNN.

The leader of the Democrats in the Senate, Chuck Schumer, slammed Stevens over her endorsement of the Republican candidate.

“This is a despicable betrayal from Representative Stevens,” he posted on X.

“Senate Democrats are united in our support for Abdul El-Sayed, because we know he will fight for the economic interests of working families in Michigan, unlike Mike Rogers, who is a tool of Donald Trump and billionaire donors.”

Meanwhile, the advocacy group Michigan Jews for Democracy has backed El-Sayed.

“Haley Stevens does not speak for Michigan’s Jewish community,” it said in a statement, which rejected her “attempt to divide our community” two days before the election.

While Democrats have been angered by Stevens’s action, Trump celebrated her decision.

During a rally in Iowa later on Sunday, the US president said he would “love” it if Stevens joined the Republican Party. “Haley said what few people are willing to say,” Trump added. “It’s a thing called bravery.”

The question now is whether Stevens’s endorsement could persuade some of her supporters to back Rogers or discourage them from voting altogether.

Polling suggested El-Sayed has largely consolidated Democratic support, according to the Reuters news agency.

Judge dismisses Trump’s Alaska election lawsuit

Meanwhile, a ⁠federal ⁠judge has thrown out a Trump administration ⁠lawsuit seeking to block Alaska from ⁠certifying a loss by Republican Senator Dan Sullivan. The administration has argued that a rival on the ballot with the same name could change the outcome.

Sullivan pledged to accept the election outcome, days after the US Department of Justice filed a lawsuit seeking to decertify the results of the Senate race if he loses.

“I’m going to accept the election results,” Sullivan, an ally of Trump, told CNN on Sunday.

Alaska’s Senate race is one of seven key toss-up races that will likely decide whether Republicans keep their majority in the upper chamber of the US Congress.

This year, out of about 210 million registered voters, 54.5 million had voted early as of 10am US East Coast time (15:00 GMT) on Sunday, according to a University of Florida analysis. This includes 30 million in-person votes and 24 million mail-in ballots.

In the 2022 midterm elections, 46 million people voted early.

Early voting enthusiasm has been higher among Democrats this year with more than 11 million registered Democrats having voted early, compared with about 8 million registered Republicans, according to the university’s analysis.

Early voting has particularly surged in the state of Texas, a key battleground, where more than 7.7 million people have voted early.

According to an Associated Press polling analysis, in South Carolina, where Trump won by nearly 18 percentage points in 2024, early voting has surged 83 percent compared with the same point in 2022. The state has open races for governor and US Senate this year.

Kansas, Michigan and Maine have also seen a surge in early voting.

Early turnout figures, however, don’t show which candidates voters have chosen or what the final results will be.

articles.title: How to watch critical 2026 midterm election races in TX, OH, MI, WI, GA, IA, NV, ME and FL
articles.summary: Nine battleground states hold the key to control of Congress as Republicans defend majorities and Democrats eye Senate pickups in the 2026 midterms.
articles.body: Control of Congress is on the line Tuesday as voters decide pivotal Senate and House races across the country, while closely watched contests for governor will shape the political landscape in key states during President Donald Trump's second term. Republicans are fighting to defend their congressional majorities as Democrats seek gains in battlegrounds from Texas and Georgia to Michigan and Maine. Open seats, vulnerable incumbents and competitive statewide races have put nine states at the center of the fight for power in Washington and state capitals. With races stretching across multiple time zones, here are the key contests to watch, when polls close and how to follow live results as Election Night unfolds. SENATE CONTROL IS A COIN FLIP — AND DEMOCRATS’ PATH RUNS THROUGH TRUMP COUNTRY Texas — Polls close at 8 p.m. ET, 9 p.m. ET in some areas Texas voters face two major statewide showdowns, with Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton battling Democratic state Rep. James Talarico for the Senate seat held by outgoing Republican John Cornyn, while GOP Gov. Greg Abbott seeks a historic fourth term against Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa. TRUMP WON THIS RELIABLY RED STATE BY DOUBLE DIGITS. NOW A DEADLOCKED RACE IS BRINGING HIM BACK The Senate contest has emerged as an unusually competitive race in a state that has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since Lloyd Bentsen in 1988, pitting Paxton's conservative appeal and history of legal controversies against Talarico's campaign focused on political change. Meanwhile, Abbott's reelection bid offers another test of Republican dominance, with border security, education and the economy shaping the fight over the state's future. Ohio — Polls close at 7:30 p.m. ET Ohio features a Senate rematch of sorts, with former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown seeking a return to Washington against Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed to fill Vice President JD Vance's former seat. Brown is attempting a political comeback in a state that has shifted toward Republicans, while Husted seeks his first electoral victory for the Senate. Husted's campaign also enlisted Ohio native and former NFL coach Jon "Chucky" Gruden for campaign appearances. Voters will decide who succeeds term-limited Republican Gov. Mike DeWine, with Republican Vivek Ramaswamy facing Democrat Amy Acton. Ramaswamy's campaign recently pulled a controversial ad featuring Acton's estranged mother after criticism from fellow Republicans, including DeWine. Michigan — Polls close at 8 p.m. ET, 9 p.m. ET in some areas Michigan's open Senate seat could prove pivotal to the balance of power in Washington, with former Republican Rep. Mike Rogers facing Democrat Abdul El-Sayed in the contest to succeed retiring Democratic Sen. Gary Peters. ABDUL EL-SAYED'S ALLEGED FAMILY TIES TO MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD SURFACE AFTER DENYING ANY LINK DURING NBC INTERVIEW The Senate race has grown increasingly contentious as Rogers and Republican allies have raised allegations about El-Sayed's family's purported ties to the Muslim Brotherhood, citing old social media posts by his half-sister. El-Sayed has denied any connection to the organization and publicly disavowed it, while independent fact-checkers have found no evidence establishing his personal affiliation. The state also features a gubernatorial showdown between Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson and Republican Rep. John James, testing whether Michigan voters will maintain Democratic control of the governor's office or turn to Republicans. Wisconsin — Polls close at 9 p.m. ET Wisconsin's open governor's race pits Republican Rep. Tom Tiffany against Democratic Milwaukee County Executive David Crowley as voters choose a successor to Democratic Gov. Tony Evers. The contest centers on the state's political direction, including taxes, public spending and education, after Crowley defeated progressive state Rep. Francesca Hong in a crowded Democratic primary. Georgia — Polls close at 7 p.m. ET Georgia offers two major statewide contests, with Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff defending his seat against Republican Rep. Mike Collins in a state Trump narrowly carried in 2024. Ossoff's race will test whether Democrats can hold a Senate seat in a state that has delivered closely contested presidential and Senate elections, while the open governor's race between Republican businessman Rick Jackson and former Democratic Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms will determine who succeeds term-limited Republican Gov. Brian Kemp. Iowa — Polls close at 9 p.m. ET Iowa voters will decide whether Republicans can retain two major offices in a state Trump carried comfortably in 2024. Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson faces Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek for the Senate seat being vacated by Republican Joni Ernst, while Democratic state Auditor Rob Sand faces Republican Zach Lahn in the open governor's race to succeed retiring longtime GOP Gov. Kim Reynolds. Although the Hawkeye State has shifted toward Republicans in recent election cycles, Democrats previously enjoyed sustained statewide success through figures including former Sen. Tom Harkin and former Gov. Tom Vilsack. The contests will test whether Democrats can regain ground, with affordability, agriculture and state economic policy among the central issues. Nevada — Polls close at 10 p.m. ET Nevada's marquee contest features Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo seeking another term against Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford. The race will test whether Republicans can retain the governor's office in a state where Democrats have remained competitive in statewide elections, with housing affordability, education and public safety among the issues facing voters. Lombardo, the former Clark County sheriff, defeated incumbent Democratic Gov. Steve Sisolak in 2022, with Ford now hoping to hit the jackpot in Carson City. Maine — Polls close at 8 p.m. ET Maine's Senate race pits longtime Republican Sen. Susan Collins against former Democratic state Senate President Troy Jackson in one of the country's most closely watched contests. Collins is seeking another term in a blue-leaning state that supported Democrat Kamala Harris in the 2024 presidential election. Meanwhile, Jackson is attempting to turn Maine's Democratic presidential voting pattern into a Senate pickup after replacing Graham Platner, who withdrew as the Democratic nominee following a sexual assault allegation that he denied. The contest will test Collins' longstanding crossover appeal and could have major consequences for the Senate's balance of power, as she remains New England's only Republican member of Congress. Florida — Polls close at 7 p.m. ET, 8 p.m. ET in some areas Florida voters will choose a successor to term-limited Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, with Republican Rep. Byron Donalds facing former Republican congressman-turned-Democrat David Jolly. The race presents a contest over the future of Florida's government, including affordability, immigration and the direction of state policy. Republican Sen. Ashley Moody, appointed to the seat vacated by Secretary of State Marco Rubio, also faces DSA-affiliated Democratic state Rep. Angie Nixon in a special Senate election, while competitive House contests could affect the national congressional picture. How to watch the 2026 midterm election results on Fox News As polls close across the country's biggest battlegrounds on Tuesday, Nov. 3, Fox News Channel and Fox News Digital will deliver live results, race calls and analysis of the contests that could determine control of Congress. Viewers can watch live coverage on Fox News Go with a participating television provider or stream Fox News Channel through FOX One. articles.title: The 5 biggest questions hanging over Election Day
articles.summary: There are no shortages of storylines to watch as the historic 2026 midterms draw to a close. The GOP is on defense as election forecasters, like Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), predict Democrats have an 82 percent chance of flipping the House and a 62 percent shot at winning the Senate. A gloomy economy, President Trump’s…
articles.body:
There are no shortages of storylines to watch as the historic 2026 midterms draw to a close.

The GOP is on defense as election forecasters , like Decision Desk HQ (DDHQ), predict Democrats have an 82 percent chance of flipping the House and a 62 percent shot at winning the Senate.

A gloomy economy, President Trump’s tanking approval ratings and opposition to the war in Iran have bogged down Republicans. But the party has sought to reinforce its winning coalition from 2024 as it casts doubt on bleak polling suggesting a pummeling Tuesday.

“The Republicans seem to be getting out their base. The Democrats are supercharged, they’re getting out their group,” said Spencer Kimball, Emerson College Polling’s executive director.

“Now we’re going to see what those independents do, if they make the difference in these races,” he added.

Here are five must-watch storylines on Election Day:

Trump has consistently urged his supporters to “pretend” that he’s on the ballot in an effort to turn out his base. Experts suggest this plea could work but that this alone won’t get Republicans across the finish line.

“I think the Trump base will come out,” Kimball said, adding that “you need the swing vote. You need those independents.”

The president has crisscrossed the country rallying for his picks in recent weeks.

Many of these stops, however, have been in red states like Alabama, Alaska, Mississippi and Kansas, setting off alarm bells for the GOP amid worries that his low approval ratings paired with high fuel and fertilizer prices could bog down the vote from independent or unaffiliated voters who supported the president last cycle.

“I don’t think you’re going to see the bottom totally fall out on Tuesday for the Republicans because Trump still does have that strong base,” Kimball added.

The polling industry has been under a microscope this cycle, and any big misses Tuesday could fan the flames.

Democrats, however, have been riding a high in the lead-up to Election Day, with rosy polling from Emerson College this past week suggesting Democrats have a 10-point lead on the generic congressional ballot.

“The polls are still telling us something — that things are a lot closer, that the environment is Democratic-leaning,” Decision Desk HQ chief election analyst Geoffrey Skelley said. “Then, it’s just a question of is it Democratic leaning enough?”

“And that’s what we won’t know until we get actual votes,” he added.

The revelation that two purported polling firms falsified data this cycle has only increased scrutiny, as Republicans argue polling this cycle is wrong .

Tighter-than-expected results from Democratic primaries this summer — including the Wisconsin gubernatorial and Michigan Senate contests — have also cast doubt on the accuracy of polling. These surveys had suggested clear front-runners in the races.

Primary polling is more difficult to conduct than general elections, but Skelley signaled the industry is on the lookout for misses in states where conducting surveys is particularly challenging.

“I think you have to be concerned about sort of larger errors in some of the same places that we’ve seen polling struggle in the Trump era, and a lot of those are states that are a part of the Senate discussion — so an Ohio or an Iowa or a Kansas potentially,” Skelley explained.

Latino voters propelled Trump’s 2024 victory, but this bloc appears to be moving back to Democrats.

While former President Biden won the bloc by 25 percentage points in 2020, Latinos took a 22-point swing toward Republicans, with the president losing them by just 3 points in 2024, according to a 2025 Pew Research Center analysis .

Now, according to a NBC News/Telemundo survey released in early October , Trump holds a 27 percent approval rating with the bloc. A separate Pew Research Center survey also released in October showed the president with a 24 percent approval rating among the bloc.

“I’m expecting that the Hispanic bloc to look more like 2008, 2012,” Kimball said, adding that he predicts the group will break for Democrats nearly 2-to-1.

Skelley, meanwhile, suggested how well Democrats perform with Latinos could depend on their turnout in a nonpresidential election year too.

Republicans have deep pockets and have dominated the war for the airwaves this cycle, outspending Democrats in the most expensive midterms ever .

The party has the added benefit of MAGA Inc., Trump’s super PAC, which has spent hundreds of millions of dollars to bolster candidates. Tesla CEO Elon Musk’s America PAC has also spent heavily to support Republicans up and down the ballot.

Kimball suggested that while money is helpful for campaigns, it remains an open question as to how much it will move the needle, particularly in the days before Election Day.

“While the money’s important and it might make a difference in some of these very close races, at this point it seems like the momentum is with the Democrats,” he added.

Democrats in battleground Senate races, for their part, have consistently posted higher fundraising hauls than their GOP rivals.

Do former swing states veer back to the center?

The president’s low approval rating and voter anger over the economy has put states like Iowa and Ohio — that voted for former President Obama twice and Trump three times — back on the map for Democrats. This sentiment has even extended to red-leaning states like Kansas, Alaska and Texas.

“Those traditional swing states that Trump has been able to carry two or three times seem to be switching back towards the Democrats,” Kimball said, underscoring Ohio.

“Generally speaking, when we grew up, it was ‘As goes Ohio, so goes the nation,'” he continued.

Democrats have largely written off Ohio in recent political memory, but this year’s different. The fiery governor’s race between Democrat Amy Acton and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy leans in Democrats’ favor, per DDHQ.

Meanwhile, control for the Senate could run through the Buckeye State where former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D) is seeking a comeback against Sen. Jon Husted (R) after his 2024 loss to GOP Sen. Bernie Moreno.

“If the Democrats are able to make inroads in either of the governor’s race or the Senate or both, that really is an indication of maybe where the country’s going,” Kimball said.

articles.title: 5 athletes and sports figures to watch on Election Day
articles.summary: This week’s midterm elections feature a handful of races involving former athletes, coaches or sports media personalities who are hoping to secure victory at the ballot box and bring their experience on or around the field of play to a role in government. Tuesday’s elections come at the end of a midterm cycle in which…
articles.body:
This week’s midterm elections feature a handful of races involving former athletes, coaches or sports media personalities who are hoping to secure victory at the ballot box and bring their experience on or around the field of play to a role in government.

Tuesday’s elections come at the end of a midterm cycle in which President Trump and the GOP especially have leaned heavily into support from athletes on the campaign trail, seeking to use sports fandom as a means of connecting with voters.

Here are five former sports figures hoping to notch a win this week and how they are expected to fare on Tuesday.

Teixeira, a former MLB slugger who won a World Series with the New York Yankees in 2009 and led the American League in home runs that year, is running for a U.S. House seat being vacated by retiring Rep. Chip Roy (R-Texas).

Texas’s 21st District, which comprises a largely rural area between San Antonio and Austin, is heavily Republican, and Teixeira is currently polling well ahead of Democratic challenger Kristin Hook.

The Republican has embraced Trump on the campaign trail and has spent time trying to boost other GOP hopefuls in the state, including state Attorney General Ken Paxton, who is in a tough Senate race with Democratic nominee James Talarico.

The party’s national leadership has called on Teixeira on a number of occasions to stump for other Republicans running for office across the country and help promote the president’s agenda as they look to defend their House and Senate majorities.

On Capitol Hill, GOP organizers of the annual congressional baseball game have expressed excitement that the team’s dominant run over Democrats on the diamond could get a major boost once Teixeira joins the team’s ranks next year, as is expected.

Tafoya is a longtime ESPN NFL sideline reporter-turned-Fox News commentator who is running as a Republican for U.S. Senate in Minnesota.

Tafoya is an underdog in the race and is facing a much harder election fight than Teixeira, with one recent polling average from Decision Desk HQ finding Democrat Peggy Flanagan leading with 47.4 percent support to Tafoya’s 43.8 percent.

Minnesota has not elected a Republican to the Senate in nearly 25 years, and Tafoya’s effort to make the state competitive for the GOP comes at a time when the GOP is facing a tough political climate.

Some political forecasters predict the former sports reporter’s embrace of Trump could ultimately hurt her in a state where a trade war with Canada and broader concerns about affordability are top of mind for many voters.

Feely spent years as an NFL kicker before joining the CBS Sports broadcast booth.

A Republican who speaks often about his faith, Feely is running in Arizona’s 1st House District against physician Amish Shah, who was once a team doctor for the New York Jets when Feely was on the team.

The Feely vs. Shah race has been in a dead heat for weeks, and some recent polls give the Democrat a slight edge in the contest to succeed Rep. Andy Biggs (R).

Feely told The Hill earlier this year the assassination attempt against Trump in Butler, Pa., inspired him to run for Congress, something he had been considering for years.

“That was a big moment for me,” he said. “I started asking myself, ‘All right, Jay. … What are you willing to sacrifice?’ It’s my time to go and serve.”

Turek is a Democrat and former Paralympic and professional basketball player who is running for Senate in Iowa against GOP Rep. Ashley Hinson.

A former European pro wheelchair basketball player, Turek has attacked Hinson over what he says is her growing wealth while serving in Congress, while she has pointed out his inconsistent attendance and voting record in the Iowa state House.

Hinson has been endorsed by Trump, while Turek in August rolled out a campaign ad that featured him and former President Obama shooting hoops. In the ad, the former president says: “I’ve seen enough. What we’ve got here is a man of character, someone who knows how to win. Now the ball’s in your court, Iowa.”

Tuberville, a U.S. senator and former NCAA football coach of the year at Auburn University, is giving up his seat to run for governor of Alabama.

He leads Democrat Doug Jones in polls by a wide margin in a state that has been a reliable stronghold for Republicans for decades.

Tuberville, who was a vocal supporter of Congress’s effort to regulate college sports this fall, beat back a residency challenge this summer that claimed he had not lived in Alabama long enough to run for the governor’s mansion.

While Trump’s decision to hold rallies in Alabama and nearby Mississippi have some Democrats hopeful the GOP could be losing support in the Deep South, Tuberville is expected to cruise to victory and win statewide office again Tuesday.

A federal judge late last week opened a misconduct probe into Trump’s Department of Justice, accusing government attorneys of lying to her as the department defends Trump’s desire to redevelop East Potomac Golf Links in court. The president has said the course will close on Nov. 15 despite an order from U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes barring future work at the property while the case is being litigated. The National Links Trust a day earlier confirmed it would cede operational control of East Potomac on Nov. 15, while Reyes has threatened to hold contempt hearings if the federal government defies her order. The judge said she would conduct the investigation herself or appoint a special master to do so.

Officials at the NCAA and major university athletic departments will be closely watching Tuesday’s midterm election results, as a shift in the congressional majorities could have major implications for the Protect College Sports Act, which was passed by the Senate before the recess. If Democrats win control of the House, Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) is expected to be elected Speaker. Jeffries has been adamant in his opposition to the NCAA’s efforts to get Congress to regulate the big business of college sports, and he vowed to lead efforts to stop it. The NAACP, Congressional Black Caucus and other groups on Capitol Hill argue the bill would disproportionately limit the earning potential of minority student-athletes.

The Golden State Valkyries secured their first WNBA title over the weekend, beating the Atlanta Dream in seven games to cap what many view as the league’s most successful season since its launch. This year’s WNBA finals, however, came under significant criticism, particularly when an elimination Game 6 was played in the daytime.

Jocks on The Hill: Rep. Jimmy Patronis (R-Fla.)

Rep. Jimmy Patronis (R-Fla.), whose family presides over panhandle seafood chain Captain Anderson’s, answered some sports questions for The Hill.

“It’s always been college football, and playing I had zero hand-eye coordination. My kids play sports, but I’m definitely a fan who enjoys watching the raw talent of amateur sports.”

“Florida State University. No questions asked. I can say things about different programs I admire. I appreciate the way Dabo Swinney conducts himself. I think there are generations of coaches that are not going to be part of the sport moving forward because the game has moved on.”

Is there an athlete you admired growing up?

“I think Josh Allen. I get emotional talking about him. I could say the same thing about Jameis Winston. You see this guy … I love when a player just pours themselves into the game and leave it all on the field to the point where a loss effects them emotionally. For my 50th birthday my sons got me a Josh Allen jersey. You see those once-in-an-era players that just inspire their teammates.”

Hate is a strong word, but is there a team you love to root against?

“I think it’s a flip of the coin between the University of Miami and the University of Florida. But you know I can’t hate … it is a strong word, but you know what, when they play against Florida State, I’m going to root against them. But when they play anybody else, I’m going to root for the Florida team.”

Sports and politics are full of cliches; is there one that resonates with you?

“You play stupid games, you win stupid prizes. We see it in the administration and the athletic department and the boosters … they got to remember it’s a different day now. A player will leave your program and go to another one for $50,000. We see the same thing in Washington all the time, and you’ve got to work through this developing moving target on fixing college sports, and we think Congress is going to be the solution, which I think is pretty comical myself.”

There has been a lot of buzz about bad blood in the “Monday Night Football” broadcast booth in recent weeks, and The Athletic’s Andrew Marchand takes a deep dive here into the “unraveling” of one of the league’s longest serving play-by-play and color commentary duos in Joe Buck and Troy Aikman.

ESPN put together a fun list that’s worth checking out, ranking the “top 10 trick plays in Super Bowl history,” which includes the famous “Philly Special” and Phil Simms’s flea-flicker to Phil McConkey in 1987.

Front Office Sports published an analysis of Federal Election Commission data that showed owners across U.S. pro sports leagues have spent more than $100 million on the midterms — mostly for Republicans.

articles.title: Democrats squabbling over how to contain Trump after Election Day
articles.summary: Democrats are expecting to win big on Election Day, but disagreements are already erupting among them over how aggressively to target President Trump for what they say are abuses of power and corruption. Democratic lawmakers and strategists are divided over whether to push another impeachment against Trump. Senators and leaders in the House are generally…
articles.body:
Democrats are expecting to win big on Election Day, but disagreements are already erupting among them over how aggressively to target President Trump for what they say are abuses of power and corruption.

Democratic lawmakers and strategists are divided over whether to push another impeachment against Trump.

Senators and leaders in the House are generally opposed to advancing a third impeachment of Trump that has virtually no chance of picking up 67 votes in the Senate — the number of votes needed to convict.

A senior Senate Democratic aide warned there is little “appetite” for holding a third Trump impeachment trial in the Senate, after previous impeachment efforts in 2020 and 2021 failed to impact Trump politically.

Democrats agree there need to be investigations of Trump and his allies next year to hold them to account, but there is little consensus over what to prioritize, according to Democratic strategists and aides.

But some senior lawmakers are warning that the party can’t get so wrapped up in tracking down the misdeeds of the president and the administration that they get pulled into too many directions or lose sight of addressing high prices and ending the war in Iran — two of the top issues of this year’s election.

“I don’t think we can ignore it,” said Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.) of the need to investigate alleged corruption in the Trump administration.

“More than 90 percent of voters think that government has been corrupted. We just have to be thoughtful and strategic about where investigative work goes and not allow that to distract us from solving fairly immediate cost problems that American families feel,” he said.

Whitehouse would become chair of the powerful Senate Judiciary Committee if Democrats win control of the Senate.

To keep their hoped-for new House majority — and possible Senate majority — from getting sucked into solely partisan battles with Trump over what has already transpired, Democratic leaders in Congress are mapping out positive agendas for the first 100 hours, the first 100 days and the first year of their new majorities, according to sources familiar with internal discussions.

Yet the desire among Democratic lawmakers to inflict retribution on Trump is strong.

Some want to delve further into the Jeffrey Epstein sex-trafficking scandal to probe whether the Justice Department violated the Epstein Files Transparency Act by withholding or improperly redacting documents.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.), who would return to the role of majority leader if Democrats capture the Senate, created a special Senate working group in February to plumb Epstein-related information held back from the public by the Trump Justice Department.

“We are demanding that the Department of Justice and the FBI preserve records on what transpired behind the scenes. We want to know who was involved in the decision to hide the truth,” he declared.

Other Democrats want to prioritize investigations of the Defense Department and the awarding of lucrative contracts linked to Donald Trump Jr.

Sens. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.), Andy Kim (D-N.J.) and Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.) sent a letter to Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth earlier this year demanding information about decisions at the Pentagon to give loans and contracts to companies “associated with the president’s son” that may have had “conflicts of interest.”

Some Democrats are pushing for investigations into the Trump family’s massive investments in the crypto industry; the president’s pardon of Binance founder and former CEO Changpeng Zhao, who pleaded guilty to violating money laundering law; and whether crypto investments provided an avenue for foreign interests to influence the president.

“We’re going to have to do voluminous oversight work because there is rampant corruption in this administration, and we need to get to the bottom of it,” said Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.).

Some Democrats want to investigate Trump’s pardon record more closely and scrutinize donations that wealthy individuals and families made in hopes of receiving clemency.

The New York Times reported that Alina Habba Mildon, one of Trump’s former lawyers, earned $50 million to help secure a pardon for the member of a wealthy Venezuelan family, among other duties.

A Democratic strategist and former House leadership aide said Democratic leaders are looking at a wide array of issues to investigate when they take back the Speaker’s gavel in January.

“Everything from corporate America and their ties to the Trump administration, Epstein, immigration,” said the strategist, noting that Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.), who would take over as chair of the House Oversight and Government Reform Committee, has been outspoken about investigating conditions at Immigration and Customs Enforcement detention facilities and immigration enforcement activities more generally.

“They’re going to spend their time looking at a variety of issues,” the strategist added, noting Democrats are “running on affordability and corruption” in the midterm election.

The House-aligned Democratic strategist said there’s little desire among House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries’s (N.Y.) leadership team to move toward another impeachment proceeding, even though there are rank-and-file members in the Democratic caucus who want to.

“I’ll tell you right now that I have not heard about impeachment, not for Trump,” the source said.

The strategist said Democratic leaders instead are eyeing a lower-key strategy to hamstring the Trump administration by tying up Cabinet and other senior officials in oversight hearings.

“That’s what they’re elected to do, to constrain Trump and to ensure that they try to get some of their agenda passed and signed into law,” the strategist said.

Beyond investigations, Democrats are threatening to make it much tougher for Trump to make appointments to the federal judiciary and the executive branch if they win control of the Senate.

And they’ve threatened to cut off funding for the war with Iran if Trump doesn’t bring the conflict to a swift conclusion.

Sen. Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii), who is set to become the next Senate Democratic whip, has warned that getting bipartisan majorities to vote for bills to authorize and fund the Pentagon will be “extremely difficult” if the war drags on.

Some Democrats, however, argue that Trump still needs to face accountability for trying to overturn the results of the 2020 presidential election or for mishandling classified documents and conspiring to obstruct justice related to those documents after leaving office in 2021.

“Donald Trump’s alleged crimes still have not been given justice. There’s been no justice yet for these alleged crimes, which are just so deeply serious, and were stopped midway in the criminal justice process,” said Blumenthal, a member of the Senate Judiciary Committee.

“I still feel there needs to be some reckoning,” he said.

Blumenthal would be poised to take over as chair of the Senate’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations if Democrats win control of the Senate this week.

Other Democrats say they want to investigate what they say has been a “corrupt relationship” between the Trump administration and wealthy special interests over the past 20 months.

Murphy says he wants to know more about “an $8 million donation made by R.J. Reynolds to the administration that resulted one week later in flavored vapes being made legal for kids.”

“We should get to the bottom of the corrupt relationship that exists between corporations in this country and the Trump administration,” he said.

articles.title: The GOP reveals a fresh $100B talking point as the battle for Congress looms
articles.summary: Kelly Loeffler says the SBA delivered $100 billion to Main Street businesses for a second straight year under Trump's tax and trade policies.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: With both parties vying to convince voters they have the better answer on the economy, Small Business Administrator Kelly Loeffler is pointing to $100 billion in support for local employers as proof that Trump’s policies are working. "We just recorded our second consecutive year of getting $100 billion to Main Street businesses," Loeffler told Fox News Digital, crediting Trump’s tax cuts, deregulation and trade policies. SMALL BUSINESS OWNERS BUILT THE AMERICAN DREAM. DEMOCRATS WANT TO TAKE IT FROM YOU The economic debate could help determine which party controls Congress, as both parties try to persuade voters their policies will improve household finances and business prospects. Loeffler said the business owners she meets want to expand but need confidence that Washington will support long-term investment. They most often tell her they need more skilled workers, she said. DSA-BACKED CANDIDATES ARE WINNING PRIMARIES AND THEIR VISION FOR AMERICA IS VERY DIFFERENT "What they can’t tolerate is having Washington say that they’re gonna massively regulate them, massively tax them," she said.
