articles.title: SCHOEN, COOPERMAN: Democrats close in as Republicans scramble to hold Congress
articles.summary: Polls, forecasts and prediction markets flash alarm bells for Republicans as Democrats eye their largest House majority since 2009 in the midterms.
articles.body: In the closing days of the 2026 midterm cycle, all available evidence suggests that the trends are moving in Democrats’ favor. Polls, forecasts, and prediction markets are now ringing alarm bells for Republicans, as virtually all key races move in Democrats’ direction. Indeed, on Saturday, Cook Political Report shifted "a dozen more House races" toward Democrats, now projecting that Democrats will flip 12-25 House seats, potentially giving them their largest majority since 2009. As a result, political forecasting sites VoteHub and Decision Desk have updated their odds of Democrats taking the House to their highest levels of the cycle: 89% and 83%, respectively, as of Sunday afternoon. EVERYTHING TO KNOW ABOUT HOUSE AND SENATE CONTROL, BALLOT MEASURES AND 2026 ELECTION DAY POLL CLOSING Prediction markets have followed suit: Kalshi gives Democrats a 93% chance to take the House and a 71% chance to win the Senate as well. To that end, the trends in the Senate point in the same direction, and while Republicans have slightly better odds of keeping the upper chamber, it’s clear that the momentum is with Democrats. SENATE CONTROL IS A COIN FLIP — AND DEMOCRATS’ PATH RUNS THROUGH TRUMP COUNTRY Final polls ahead of the election show all or most of the seven key races shifting to the left, including in Kansas, where Democrat Adam Hamilton leads in the four most recent polls, including one from The Washington Post in which he led Republican incumbent Roger Marshall by 9%. True, that is an outlier — and its accuracy is being reviewed by The Washington Post — but the fact that every other poll is within six points in a state that has not had a Democratic senator in over 90 years indicates that the underlying trend is moving in Democrats’ favor. MAINE, KANSAS SENATE RACES NECK AND NECK AS DEMOCRATS LEAD IN TEXAS, MICHIGAN, POLL SHOWS Other Republican-held seats in South Carolina, Iowa, Maine, Texas and Ohio are also increasingly within reach for Democrats. Of those races, South Carolina and Iowa are the only two where the Republican candidate has a polling lead, but it’s under three points in South Carolina and under one point in Iowa. Thus, both races are statistically tied and within reach for Democrats. GOP SENATE MAJORITY FACES FRESH UNCERTAINTY AS 2 KEY RACES TIGHTEN DAYS BEFORE MIDTERMS In the other states — Maine, Texas, Ohio and Michigan — the polls have consistently shown Democratic candidates leading. And while those leads are small, they have not contracted, and Michigan in particular has seen a noticeable widening, with Abdul El-Sayed now leading Republican Mike Rogers by roughly four points. However, it will be interesting to see whether Rep. Haley Stevens’ endorsement of Rogers impacts the race, particularly among moderates and Black voters, as polls show that El-Sayed has struggled with both key demographics. DEMOCRAT HALEY STEVENS ENDORSES GOP SENATE NOMINEE MIKE ROGERS AT DETROIT CHURCH That said, given that North Carolina’s Senate race is effectively decided for Democrat Roy Cooper — who leads Republican Michael Whatley by nearly 11 points — Democrats now have a wide range of possible routes to winning the Senate. VETERAN DEM OPERATIVE SAYS SUBPAR GOP CANDIDATES POISED TO HAND OVER SENATE MAJORITY Immediately after the 2024 election, it may have seemed improbable that just two years later, Democrats would be on the verge of retaking both the House and Senate, let alone possibly winning states like South Carolina, Alaska, Iowa, Texas and Kansas. Yet it is a very real possibility, owing in no small part to President Trump’s approval rating, currently below 40%. SCHOEN, COOPERMAN: DEMOCRATS COULD BE RIDING A MIDTERM WAVE. THESE NUMBERS SHOULD TERRIFY THE GOP On key issues, it’s even worse. Less than 3 in 10 (29%) Americans approve of Trump’s handling of the economy, and an even smaller 22% approve of how he’s handled inflation, per Fox News polling. Even as Republican candidates and operatives talk up their chances in these close races, there are signs of panic within Republican ranks. TRUMP-BACKED SENATOR ADMITS GOP FACES NIGHTMARE SCENARIO IN STATE REPUBLICANS HAVEN'T LOST IN 90 YEARS Trump’s decision to cancel then reschedule rallies in Kansas and Iowa this weekend says as much. Republicans in those two deep-red states should not need a boost from the president, but with the national environment tilting toward Democrats, they do. CLICK HERE FOR MORE FOX NEWS OPINION Put another way, if Republicans were confident in their chances, they would not need the president to campaign in some of the deepest-red states and districts. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Ultimately, while we will only know the true picture after all the votes have been counted, coming out of the campaign’s final weekend, it is clear that Democrats have the advantage. Carly Cooperman is CEO of Schoen Cooperman Research. CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM DOUG SCHOEN CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM CARLY COOPERMAN

articles.title: Pink slime newsrooms are the fake news operations we need to talk about
articles.summary: The place where voters increasingly get their news has been infected by propaganda cleverly designed to imitate the one type of journalism voters still trust.
articles.body:
We are at the confluence of two disquieting events.

The first is that local news remains the only form of journalism voters still largely trust , a sharp contrast to the public’s very dim opinion of newspaper and television reporting. This is good for local journalism, especially amid its national gutting. But it is not particularly healthy that the national press — supposedly our most powerful watchdogs — are so widely distrusted.

The second is the little-noticed expansion, over the last two decades, of the pink slime economy.

Taken together, the two suggest we are heading for a genuine information crisis.

For the uninitiated, NewsGuard describes “pink slime” as “sites that present themselves as professional news outlets but are secretly backed by partisan groups with a clear though undisclosed agenda.” Along with phony stories and websites, the operators behind these schemes often pay Meta large sums to advertise their “reports” across users’ newsfeeds, generating millions upon millions of impressions.

The stories — generally low-quality, low-effort, and often misleading, either directly or by omission — exist to target specific voter demographics, swing states and candidates. The result is an audience tricked into mistaking political advertising for honest reporting, with voters’ preferences subtly influenced.

Social media is positively lousy with these reports. And unfortunately, the problem has only worsened in recent years, according to a recent study by Carnegie Mellon University .

The number of these pink slime sites ballooned from roughly a handful in 2006 to an estimated 1,200 today .

The practice dates to at least George W. Bush’s first term, with the appearance of the Madison County Record in Illinois, which presented itself as a genuine news organization despite its undisclosed ties to the U.S. Chamber of Commerce.

Then, in 2018, the left-wing States Newsroom launched , eventually establishing operations in all 50 states and earning a pink slime designation from NewsGuard . States Newsroom disputes the label.

By 2019 there were an estimated 450 such sites, “each distributing thousands of algorithmically generated articles and a smaller number of reported stories,” according to the Columbia Journalism Review . Of these sites, at least 42 percent belonged to the right-leaning Metric Media, which had launched that same year.

The left-leaning Courier Newsroom also launched in 2019, founded by former CBS News and 60 Minutes staffer Tara McGowan. McGowan, who has the Obama-era slogan “Yes, we can” tattooed on her left arm , raised around $25 million from left-wing donors to produce several of these phony news websites after President Trump’s first election. The explicit purpose was to pass off Democratic Party propaganda as genuine reporting. McGowan’s get-out-the-vote nonprofit, Acronym, funded Courier Newsroom through April 2021 .

As of this writing, the largest pink slime network belongs to Metric Media. It boasts an estimated 1,100 standalone websites , dwarfing the approximately 130 combined left-wing sites run by groups such as Courier and States Newsroom. But a numbers advantage does not necessarily mean a spending advantage. Where Metric Media outnumbers left-leaning pink slime operations in standalone sites, Courier outstrips everyone in money spent promoting content on Facebook, netting millions of impressions.

Since its founding, Courier Newsroom has spent an estimated $8 million total on Facebook ads — the most of any network by a large margin, according to the CMU study . Metric Media has spent only $2 million on Meta ads during the same period. A newer left-leaning entity, American Independent, has spent an estimated $813,000 on its Facebook presence since its launch in 2022.

These website and spending figures don’t even account for the smaller pink-slime pop-ups — entities that appear practically overnight to influence a single election cycle and then disappear. This includes the left-leaning Main Street Sentinel, created in February 2022 and inactive after February 2023 after spending roughly $1.4 million on Meta advertising during the midterm elections. This also includes the left-leaning Morning Mirror, which materialized suddenly to disseminate pro-Democratic propaganda in Pennsylvania, Florida, Michigan, and Wisconsin. It spent up to $381,000 on Meta ads and then ceased meaningful activity immediately after the 2024 presidential election.

Regardless of which ideological cohort spends more, one thing is clear across CMU’s data: pink slime ad spending has increased steadily across the board, with brief but sharp spikes in election years. Total Facebook ad spending for all pink slime organizations in 2018 was just $21,713. In 2024 the combined total was $7.9 million .

The pink slime journalistic economy, then, has grown exponentially in the last 20 years, not only in number and spending but in reach beyond social media. Its fruits are visible even now on the 2026 campaign trail, with pink slime stories appearing in certain campaign ads. In Ohio, for example, a PAC ran an ad against Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), quoting the Ohio Capital Journal’s negative characterization of him as the energy companies’ “ golden boy .” What the ad does not disclose is that the Ohio Capital Journal is not an independent news organization, but part of the left-leaning States Newsroom’s pink slime network.

In Alabama’s 2nd congressional district, an ad in support of Republican candidate Rhett Marques (R) cited Yellowhammer News to credit the candidate with creating “$1.5 billion in tax relief .” The ad failed to mention that Yellowhammer is co-owned by a conservative political consultant whose clients include the Marques campaign .

There is a reason these groups disguise themselves as legitimate local news organizations rather than national news outlets. Although major media continue to suffer an existential credibility crisis, voters still largely trust local journalism. More specifically, 70 percent of U.S. adults say they have “a lot of” or “some trust” in local news, according to Pew .

Pew also found that 88 percent of U.S. adults now say they get their news “often” or “at least sometimes” from digital devices. Meanwhile, the preference for getting local journalism online versus on television has increased in recent years .

In other words, the place where voters increasingly get their news has been infected by propaganda cleverly designed to imitate the one tiny space within journalism that they still trust. It is as simple and as devious as that.

When we talk about electioneering and dirty tricks, this is not primarily about foreign online bots. Pink slime is far more intelligent, targeted, dedicated, complex, and, for all we know, better funded than any goofy meme .

Much more dangerous than memes or dimwitted podcasters are the complex networks of partisan agitprop worming their way into the newsfeeds of unsuspecting voters — networks that combine the journalism know-how of their founders with keen algorithmic tools to game social media feeds and prop up or attack political candidates, all while trading on the good name of the last form of trusted journalism.

Becket Adams is a journalist and media critic in Washington.

articles.title: Voters fear the America they've known is slipping away. On that, the left and right agree
articles.summary: The stakes in Tuesday’s midterm elections are so high that Shane Dunn voted for the first time in his life, at age 65. After a career as a cook up and down t...
articles.body:
The stakes in Tuesday's midterm elections are so high that Shane Dunn voted for the first time in his life, at age 65.

After a career as a cook up and down the East Coast, Dunn moved to the Philadelphia suburbs and voted last week in Levittown. "I was always a busy man," he said outside his polling place. But now, "I'm learning what's going on within our country, and this is actually what brought me out."

Democrats got his vote. "It feels great, to put my word in," he said, patting the "I Voted" sticker on his black hoodie.

Voters across the United States are getting their word in, too, as they determine which party controls the Senate and the House and takes charge of governors' offices, legislatures and state leadership posts in the final two years of Republican Donald Trump's presidency .

What many of them see is that the America they've known is slipping away.

They see lawlessness coming from those who create the laws. They see hate stirred by politicians among neighbors, corruption at every turn, billionaires ruling the roost and a culture that doesn't speak to how they live — in short, American bedrock at risk of crumbling. Not to mention those crazy gas prices .

In dozens of Associated Press interviews with people who cast ballots at advance polling places or drop boxes across the country, the angst was palpable, most sharply from those who oppose Trump but also from many who support him.

"I saw my vote today as trying to put the brakes on just the madness," said Arthur Horner, 59, who runs a food importing and marketing company that has been hurt by tariffs , after dropping his mail ballot at Dauphin County's election bureau in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. He voted for Democrats.

In Sioux City, Iowa, cattle rancher Elizabeth Marlett, 61, voted in Woodbury County's historic Prairie-style courthouse and walked out stewing about a variety of things — the chemicals in processed food, her son's struggles to get his veterans' benefits and, perhaps most of all, what she sees as society's leftward lurch. Things seem broken to her, too.

"Family values are going by the wayside, and they need to be brought back," she said. "Our liberties have been stomped all over. Religion has been stomped all over. And I believe we in the majority need to step up and stop being silent." She voted Republican.

Voters despair at the stoking of anger by Trump and allies

The anger in the air, stirred by a cursing president who abides no slights, is too much for some people.

"He's just destroying us," Democrat Linda Markle, 72, said of the president. She spoke outside the Warminster Township library in Bucks County, Pennsylvania.

"I am so afraid for this country," she said. "People used to look out for each other. Not anymore."

"All people do now is just hate each other," she said, and Trump "seems to have given them the courage to go ahead and be like that. … The division is horrible, absolutely horrible, and I can't wait to see the back of him."

Republican Chris Smith, 27, a Harrisburg software engineer who voted for Trump in 2024, sympathizes with Markle's sentiment, to a point.

"A lot of people hate him for various reasons, and I can understand why," he said, noting that "I think he's kind of going a bit crazy on a lot of things." But he likes Trump's effort to return manufacturing to the U.S. along with the goals of his tariffs, and he voted Republican because he still thinks that party is more fiscally responsible than Democrats.

In Ohio, Lori Wilkinson, a retired home health worker from New Pittsburg, and her husband, David, a janitor, consider themselves independents. David recently wrote to their Republican governor, Mike DeWine, to tell him what a good job he's doing, and they voted for Republican George W. Bush for president in the past.

Trump? "He's the worst president in United States history," David said from the Wayne County election center. "You get up every day, and you're like, 'What's he going to do now?'" Said Lori: "He's got the hate just so bad, it's just out of hand. It's just out of control." She fears that if Democrats win widely Tuesday, Trump will "go fricking berserk."

Trump supporter Therese Mennell gets it. "There's that kind of arrogant vibe about him that people don't like, and sometimes I shut him off because of the way he talks," the retiree said from the Wayne County center. "But, I mean, he's doing the right thing. He is saving our country."

Despite his striking unpopularity in polls, Trump repeatedly asked supporters to pretend he's on the midterm ballot, betting that would motivate fans to vote who otherwise might not. But that cuts both ways.

Samontae Mwangi, 20, and his brother, Gathenya Mwangi, 19, voted for the first time, casting early ballots Tuesday at their election center in Topeka, Kansas. Both work at a plant that manufactures trackside buildings for railroads.

They went with their grandfather, Lynn Henderson, 68, a retired Goodyear Tire and Rubber Co. worker and a former Marine lance corporal who wore a Marine's cap. Henderson said he took his grandsons to vote because his own mother died recently and he wanted them to have an event to remember him when he's gone.

All three are hoping that the election produces Democratic victories and political change. Gathenya said the economy and discontent with Trump could motivate people who've voted in the past to show up, as well as those who never have. "It really could change, make a difference, I feel, if a lot of people vote," he said.

Denise Wunder, a retired sandwich shop manager, pulled up to the center in a van featuring a decorative license plate with an American eagle. The strong Trump supporter is the daughter of Democrats. Illegal immigration is her top issue.

"I think Trump is kind of our last hope, because otherwise this world's going to go to hell in a handbasket," she said. "Yeah, he says stupid stuff, but, you know, so do we."

In the Richmond, Virginia, suburb of Henrico County, voters arrived at a steady clip on a crisp fall afternoon a week from Election Day. The moment of decision found one conservative couple, Joan and Frank Bark, lamenting the country's direction.

"I'm afraid Trump has gotten so egotistical, it's affecting his ability to make intelligent or more favorable decisions," Frank said. But, he said, "I don't want the decisions that would be generated from that far left side, either."

Joan, a retiree like her husband, said of Democrats: "I haven't found very much that they want to change or work with. It's just mostly, 'I hate Trump.'" But Trump really isn't on the ballot. They voted for Republican candidates.

In Nanuet, New York, people streamed into the small room of a community center to vote; some were in Halloween costumes. Primrose D. Sullivan, a nurse, is an independent. She scoffed at Trump's wish that voters act as if he's running.

"No, because he's not," she said. "When a patient comes into the hospital, you want me dealing in facts, not in, 'Hmm, let me act like you might have cancer.' No. Do you or do you not have cancer? We need to proceed based on facts." She voted for Democrats.

Yet some see a cancer on politics, if not the presidency

Sullivan was among a number of voters who singled out the billionaires Trump has made common cause with and how that might feed into American decline.

"I don't begrudge any of our wealthy people, Jeff Bezos or, you know, Elon Musk," she said. "But I do have a certain problem with them wanting more and more and doing things that really don't help humanity."

"If we keep going the way these guys are going," she went on, meaning both the political and CEO classes, "we're not going to have anything like what we had in the past." Theirs is a "self-destructive attitude," she added, "because, honestly, if the whole planet destroys itself, the wealthy go with us."

Outside the polling station at the YMCA in Fort Mill, South Carolina, Benjamin Updegraft offered a piercing denunciation of the elite as he traced his evolution from a "full-throated young Republican" who voted for Trump as a young man in 2016 to a "lifetime Democrat," after casting his ballot in the Senate race.

He cited Musk's throttling of his Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, which disrupted a key defense against Russian attacks, and Republican Vivek Ramaswamy's ad in the Ohio governor's race featuring the estranged mother of Democratic rival Amy Acton among the reasons powerful men must be brought to heel.

"That needs to be cut out from this country like a cancer," Updegraft said. "We have an incredible responsibility to take back the stranglehold that the worst people in this country have on the reins of power and to inflict punishment on them for their actions."

In Scottsdale, Arizona, David Lee described his conservative upbringing, his past voting for Republicans and now his decision to turn against that party and vote Democratic in the contested races for governors and the House. He considers Trump's heavy-handed immigration enforcement to be lawless.

"Nobody wants open borders, but you're treating these people without due process, sending people to countries they don't even belong to," said Lee, 63. "There's no more rules."

Then there are those prices. And that war

The Trump supporters interviewed by the AP at the polls signaled their tolerance of the surge of gas prices from the Iran war , in some cases blaming factors other than the actual cause. Nor did they break with him on the war itself .

Among them was David Stouffer, 59, branch manager for a mortgage bank and three-time Trump voter, who spoke outside the Harrisburg elections office. "Iran has been killing Americans for 50 freaking years," he said. "Yeah, I'll suffer with some higher gas prices in the interim until they get that nonsense figured out."

Does that put a crunch on your household budget, Stouffer was asked. "Of course it does." How to cope with that? "I just keep driving."

"He's made the tax cuts real," Stouffer said. "He has secured the borders. That, to me, is a very, very big deal."

By the dozens, Democrats, independents and Republicans outside the core of Trump's support differed with that assessment, even as some of them granted the president his achievements on taxes and immigration.

Horner, the food importer, is going "bonkers" with the tariffs and all the other moves bouncing between the Trump administration and the courts while a "feckless" and now electorally endangered Republican Congress largely stands aside.

"You can't do business when every month you have to readjust your pricing because the president gets a wild hair on something that he's not even constitutionally allowed to do," Horner said. He added, "He's just playing out the clock on all of this stuff — where you just know he knows it's wrong.

"And what do we have? Higher healthcare, higher food, higher gas, a business environment that is complete chaos."

But Jerry Casner, 74, of Mechanicsburg, a suburb of Harrisburg, wants as much of Trump as he can get. Alas, "he can't run again," Casner noted.

"Well, technically," Casner said, "he can't run again."

Hanna reported from Topeka, Kan.; Levy from Harrisburg, Pa.; Catalini from Levittown, Pa.; and Woodward from Washington. articles.title: Stevens shocks Democrats with last-minute Rogers endorsement
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ A November surprise ▪ Judge tosses DOJ Alaska suit ▪ Murphy recovering from stroke ▪ Daylight saving time ends Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) dropped a bombshell in the Michigan Senate race as she threw her support behind Republican Mike Rogers just two days before Election Day. The congresswoman had originally been…
articles.body:
Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) dropped a bombshell in the Michigan Senate race as she threw her support behind Republican Mike Rogers just two days before Election Day.

The congresswoman had originally been scheduled to appear with Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed at a rally brokered by Democratic Reps. James Clyburn (S.C.) and Debbie Dingell (Mich.) designed to smooth over tensions between the primary opponents. But El-Sayed disinvited Stevens from the event after she criticized him online and urged him to condemn an ad blaming U.S. support for Israel for the high cost of groceries.

The ad was produced by an outside progressive group and not El-Sayed’s campaign. El-Sayed has distanced himself from it and said he didn’t agree with the content but stopped short of a full condemnation.

“Abdul was very clear. He said, ‘Don’t come,’” Stevens said Sunday.

Instead, Stevens began her day with an appearance with Rogers for a service at Detroit’s Perfecting Church before endorsing him. She cited various factors, including El-Sayed’s past campaign appearance with controversial left-wing Twitch streamer Hasan Piker .

“As you may have seen, our Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Abdul, said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign, and that I should stay away. And he’s right. And that’s why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today,” she said in a video posted to social media Sunday.

CNN host Anderson Cooper pressed Stevens on Sunday night about what changed since she wrote in an X post in August that, “Mike Rogers will be another rubber stamp for Donald Trump’s dangerous agenda. We can’t afford to give MAGA another Senate seat in November.”

“Well, why is it OK to have the Democratic Party and a top nominee, you know, ejecting, you know, this type of, or injecting rather, this type of anger and lack of kindness?” she replied.

The reaction from fellow Democrats has been swift and furious. Multiple members of Stevens’s office, including her longtime chief of staff, resigned following her decision.

“Haley Stevens’ decision to campaign with Rogers—a man who has repeatedly sold out Michigan’s working class, wants to pass a national abortion ban, and has pledged to be a loyal vote for [President] Trump ’s agenda—shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about,” said Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel .

Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin (Mich.) said in a statement on X, “ anyone who makes an election this important about themselves, and not Michiganders and our democracy, should think hard about whether they are serving the greater good.”

Politico reported that several House Democrats said they support removing Stevens from the caucus or having leadership punish her somehow over the endorsement.

Stevens defended her decision in comments to reporters.

“It’s my personal and private decision. I still love the party. I’ve done a ton for the party,” Stevens said. “I’ve voted for the party over and over and over again. I’m going to continue to do that as I fill out my term. Everyone should be fired up for Democrats.”

Rogers needs the help, if polls are any indication.

The final New York Times/Siena poll of the cycle, released on Sunday, showed El Sayed up 11 points on the former congressman. Decision Desk HQ gives El Sayed a 76 percent chance of replacing Sen. Gary Peters (D), and he leads Rogers in the polling average by about 4.5 points.

Still, the gap is generally within the margin of error, and a small polling error could result in a big change in the outcome.

Rogers welcomed Stevens’s support, saying he was “honored” by her endorsement. He called it an example of “courage in politics.”

El-Sayed, meanwhile, brushed off the endorsement , saying he’s focused on issues in his state.

“This is a state of 10 million people who deserve a lot better from the government. I’m a lot more focused on the 9,999,998 that are not the ones you guys are talking about,” he told reporters.

Democrats need to net at least four seats to win back control, and a loss in the Great Lakes State would only make the job harder. The party went through a divisive primary between the progressive El-Sayed and moderate Stevens that was ultimately decided by less than 1 percentage point.

Whether the endorsement will have much of an effect is just one of many questions hanging over Election Day. The Hill’s Caroline Vakil dives into other key questions and storylines to watch as votes come in. Insiders can sign up and read here .

▪ The Hill : Five races that will tell the story of the midterms.

▪ The Hill : The six races that could decide Senate control.

CALL FOR NOMINATIONS : The Hill is currently collecting nominations for its annual Top Lobbyists list, made up of the most influential folks in Washington. Know a lobbyist who moved the needle this year? Nominate them for The Hill’s Top Lobbyists here by Friday, Nov. 6.

Trump will deliver remarks this afternoon at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, reportedly focusing on an update on his various projects around the nation’s capital and a closing message promoting the administration’s accomplishments ahead of the midterms.

Democrats edged out their Republican opponents in seven key battleground Senate races in the final polls from The New York Times and Siena University. Still, most of the results were within the margin of error.

All nine passengers traveling in a business jet have been confirmed dead after the plane nose-dived into a South Florida neighborhood Sunday. There were no immediate reports of deaths or injuries on the ground. An investigation into what happened is underway.

Competing yard signs for Mary Peltola, the Democratic candidate in Alaska’s Senate race, and incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) are seen on Oct. 31, 2026, in Anchorage, Alaska. (AP Photo/Lindsey Wasson)

DISMISSED : A federal judge has tossed the Justice Department’s lawsuit challenging the results of Alaska’s Senate race if a second candidate named Dan Sullivan leads to Democrats flipping the seat.

Democrat Mary Peltola , a former congresswoman, is seeking to oust Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska) in one of the most critical Senate contests of the cycle. The New York Times reported last week that Peltola’s campaign recruited Daniel J. Sullivan , a retired teacher, as a ploy to help take votes away from the incumbent.

Even before that report, the controversy led to a preemptive lawsuit from the Justice Department. U.S. District Judge Sharon Gleason ruled Sunday the administration hadn’t shown how she could rectify their concerns, noting that ballots have already been prepared and the election is Tuesday.

The Alaska Supreme Court has already signed off on the other Sullivan’s candidacy.

The administration plans to appeal the ruling. Separately, Alaska Gov. Mike Dunleavy (R) has ordered an investigation into the situation and indicated that certification of the election could be delayed based on the probe’s finding.

If Peltola wins a close vote, the legal fight looks set to escalate.

▪ The Hill : Sullivan says he will accept results.

▪ The Hill : Judge dismisses Trump suit against Wall Street Journal again.

▪ The Hill : State supreme court races to watch Tuesday.

RESPONDING WELL : Sen. Chris Murphy (D-Conn.) is recovering after suffering a stroke over the weekend.

Murphy’s chief of staff, Allison Herwitt , said the senator started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son’s hockey game Saturday and was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered that he had a stroke. He was transferred to Johns Hopkins University’s hospital for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment, she said.

Herwitt said Murphy is awake and alert and expected to make a full recovery. Murphy has served in the Senate since 2013 and was reelected to a third term in 2024.

▪ The Hill : Plan for lame-duck sprint in Congress runs into obstacles.

OFF RAMP? Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth may have an exit strategy from the administration as Sen. Marsha Blackburn ‘s (R-Tenn.) bid to become governor of Tennessee will likely leave a Senate seat vacant.

Two sources familiar with the matter told The Hill’s Filip Timotija that Hegseth is interested in the open seat, while another source said he’s campaigning behind the scenes for it. A fourth source who works closely with the Pentagon said his interest is an open secret.

The report comes as Hegseth seems to be at the top of Democrats’ list of administration officials to conduct oversight on should they retake control of one or both chambers of Congress.

Two sources regularly in the Pentagon said questions are swirling inside the department over how long Hegseth lasts in his current role even if he’s not impeached. The Pentagon’s press secretary dismissed Hegseth’s interest in the Senate as “beltway gossip by anonymous sources.”

Blackburn has indicated that if she wins the gubernatorial race, she plans to name her successor.

▪ The Hill : Congress’s defense bill streak could be in jeopardy.

▪ CNN : Hegseth’s future could be on the line if Democrats win the House.

The president will participate in telerallies at 11 a.m. and 11:45 a.m. He will deliver remarks at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool at 2 p.m. He will participate in seven additional telerallies through the rest of the day, starting at 4 p.m. until the last one at 8:15 p.m.

The House will convene at 2 p.m. for a pro forma session.

The Senate will meet at 4:30 p.m. for a pro forma session.

Clockmaker Scott Gow adjusts the hands of a clock at the Electric Time Company on Oct. 30, 2024, in Medfield, Mass. (AP Photo/Charles Krupa)

FALLING BACK : Daylight saving time came to an end Sunday as most of the country switched their clocks back an hour. Trump hopes it won’t happen again.

The president has gone all in advocating for the Sunshine Protection Act, which would make daylight saving time permanent year-round, ending the biannual clock changes. The legislation passed the House earlier this year, but the Senate has yet to take it up despite a pressure campaign from the president.

The Hill’s Mallory Wilson reports how the debate has grown divisive even within the GOP.

Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.), generally a staunch ally of the president, has become a chief critic of the proposal, expressing concern about the late sunrises that would result from permanent daylight saving time.

“Arkansans don’t want their kids going to school in the pitch dark, and I’ll always put Arkansas first,” he wrote in a post on X last month.

Trump recently touted the push at a rally in Mississippi last week, calling the time change “ridiculous.” He pointed to data showing less crime is committed when there’s more light in the evening.

But Wilson notes that supporters of both sides can point to data to back their case.

Meanwhile, Senate Majority Leader John Thune (R-S.D.) doesn’t seem eager to move the bill quickly, saying it doesn’t have a clear path to pass. Whether a Democratic majority would be more inclined to move on it remains uncertain.

▪ The Hill : Trump says he’ll become ‘Mr. Veto’ if Democrats win Congress.

Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar (“Straight”) party, waves to supporters following the release of the first exit poll results in Israel’s general election in Tel Aviv, Israel, on Oct. 28, 2026. (AP Photo/Baz Ratner)

COME TOGETHER : Israeli opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot appears to be making some inroads toward replacing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu ‘s government, though obstacles remain.

Eisenkot is set to meet with the leaders of the other parties in his bloc this week for the first time since Israel’s parliamentary elections last week to coordinate their strategy, Haaretz reported . He received a boost over the weekend as one of the top leaders of Joint List, a coalition of Arab political parties, said his group was prepared to support the bloc to replace Netanyahu’s government.

Yousef Jabareen , the party’s chairman, said initial contacts have been made with the leaders of the anti-Netanyahu coalition.

But he declined Eisenkot’s call to declare Hamas a terrorist organization, one of four conditions that Eisenkot has laid out for members of the Knesset to join him in a government. A senior Joint List member, Ahmad Tibi , emphasized that it would support the government but did not want to be part of it.

With the results of the Israeli election finalized, the opposition bloc led by Eisenkot won 48 seats of the Knesset. Netanyahu’s coalition won 53, while the two Arab groups won 19. None won enough alone for a majority of the parliament’s 120 seats.

Eisenkot would have a path to a majority through working with the Arab parties, but other members of his bloc have ruled out forming a coalition with them.

Israeli President Isaac Herzog will decide whether Eisenkot or Netanyahu gets the first chance to form a governing coalition.

▪ The Hill : Democrats weigh Israeli election results amid uncertainty.

▪ The Associated Press : Officials say results will stand despite Netanyahu’s claims.

The polling average won. Now what? Jon Cohen writes in The Hill.

Will Tuesday be a blue wave or just an anti-Trump surge? Douglas MacKinnon writes in The Hill.

The Golden State Valkyries celebrate their win over the Atlanta Dream in Game 7 of the WNBA basketball finals on Oct. 31, 2026, in San Francisco. (AP Photo/Tony Avelar)

And finally … History was made in the WNBA on Saturday as the Golden State Valkyries won Game 7 of the finals to become the fastest team to ever win a championship in league history.

The Valkyries defeated the Atlanta Dream by a score of 68-63 to clinch the series, four games to three. The championship came in just the Valkyries’ second year as a franchise, the quickest any team has won it all after their creation.

They are just the third team ever across the NBA, WNBA and former Basketball Association of America to win the finals within their first two seasons, ESPN reported . The win brings an end to the WNBA’s 30th season, which saw record viewership and attendance as the league moves into the mainstream.

articles.title: Michigan Dem claims Stevens shot down Rogers endorsement rumor hours before turning on El-Sayed
articles.summary: Haley Stevens told Rep. Debbie Dingell at midnight the Rogers endorsement was just a rumor. Five hours later, she stood beside him at a Detroit church.
articles.body: The decision by Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., to endorse Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers was apparently a sudden change of heart, and tied to the Abdul El-Sayed campaign's stay-away order this weekend. Rep. Debbie Dingell, D-Mich., said Stevens told her Saturday night that reports of an impending Rogers endorsement were not accurate. "It's very hard," Dingell told local FOX 2 on Sunday night. "Haley Stevens told me at midnight last night this was all a rumor and was not true." DEMOCRAT HALEY STEVENS ENDORSES GOP SENATE NOMINEE MIKE ROGERS AT DETROIT CHURCH Five hours later, Stevens was standing shoulder to shoulder with Rogers at a Detroit church service. "She texted me at 7:45, watching you on MS NOW, heart, heart," Dingell continued. "And by the way, I talked to her. Look, I'm just upset. I'm very concerned. It's sad, but I don't want to be distracted anymore." The Detroit church event was intended to bring unity for El-Sayed's campaign, because Stevens had won the Black vote, but instead, after being told by the Democratic nominee to stay away, she unified with Rogers. FORMER RIVAL DODGES FULL-THROATED EL-SAYED ENDORSEMENT AFTER BITTER SENATE PRIMARY "We got a phone call this morning and, you know, there's been a lot of unfortunate activity, I think," Rogers told FOX 2 Detroit. "Abdul discarded Haley Stevens, was rude to Haley Stevens, has been rude, I think, to many in the African-American community. At least that's what they're telling me. And I think this just boiled over when he dis-invited her to the campaign event that was supposed to happen today. And basically said don't need you and don't need your supporters." Rogers welcomed the early November surprise with just two days to go before Tuesday's Election Day in a race that could flip the Democratic Senate seat red and help President Donald Trump's party keep control of the upper chamber. HALEY STEVENS RIPPED BY FELLOW DEMS FOR REFUSING TO EXPLICITLY BACK EL-SAYED: 'STAY THE F--- OFF TELEVISION' "I think she picked up the phone today after having lots of, apparently, conversations with a lot of people and picked up a phone and said, 'Hey, I heard you’re going to church, you want some company?'" Rogers added. "And so that was, I mean, we were very welcome for her, I’m very welcome to have her support." The unity event became divisive for the former Democratic Senate primary combatants after Stevens called on El-Sayed to condemn an outside group’s ad that she said blamed Israel for high grocery prices. Stevens' fiancé Jason Turkish, a Democratic donor and Jewish lawyer, said earlier in the week that he was going to vote for Rogers, raising concern from El-Sayed's campaign and other Democrats. ROGERS OPENS DOOR TO DEMOCRATIC VOTERS AFTER EL-SAYED’S PRIMARY VICTORY: ‘THERE IS STILL HOPE’ El-Sayed’s campaign then asked Stevens to skip his events through Election Day to avoid distracting from the race, sources said. In a social media video, Stevens said, "I don’t belong in Abdul’s campaign." Rogers said Democrats were "veering off into the virulent hate" directed at a group of people, while Stevens’ mother, Maria Marcotte, told Reuters her daughter was concerned about rhetoric she believed frightened constituents. BLACK VOTERS, JEWISH DEMOCRATS IN MICHIGAN WARY OF VOTING FOR EL-SAYED, SAY 'HE'S TAKING ADVANTAGE' Despite the rift, El-Sayed’s campaign said it raised $1.2 million in the four hours after Stevens’ endorsement, its second-best fundraising day since the August primary. Fox News Power Rankings' latest projection rates the race as a Toss Up. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 Senate majority. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP While midterm election history tends to deliver power back to the party in the minority, Trump and Republicans have put added emphasis on retaining Senate control to hold back what is expected to become a Democrat-controlled House. Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: Trump takes midterm campaign blitz to historic stage for grand finale before Election Day
articles.summary: President Donald Trump brings his whirlwind midterm campaign to a close in Washington, D.C., after weeks of rallies, celebrity appearances and memorable moments on the road.
articles.body: President Donald Trump is set to deliver his closing midterm campaign message Monday at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, D.C., capping a weekslong campaign blitz that has taken him across more than 20 states as Republicans fight to maintain control of Congress in Tuesday's elections. Trump is scheduled to speak at 2 p.m. ET and participate in nine tele-rallies throughout the day, following in-person campaign stops in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday. The president has made 30 in-person political appearances since August, including more than 27 rallies in October, with a longtime adviser who has joined him on the road offering a behind-the-scenes look at the travel, logistics and memorable moments along the way. LEAVITT SAYS TRUMP IS DEFYING MIDTERM HEADWINDS AS HE BARNSTORMS COUNTRY Alex Bruesewitz, a senior adviser to Trump's 2024 presidential campaign who has accompanied him on roughly 10 to 15 trips in recent weeks, told Fox News Digital that organizing rallies for a sitting president presents challenges far different from those of a traditional campaign. "It's actually much different than the campaign," Bruesewitz said. "When you're doing an event moving the current president of the United States, the logistics that go into it are nuts." The operation requires extensive coordination among White House staff, Republican operatives, campaign aides and advance teams, with the White House Office of Political Affairs, Office of Public Liaison and Republican National Committee all playing roles, according to Bruesewitz. "President Trump will continue crisscrossing the country with unmatched energy and enthusiasm to deliver a simple message: with Republicans in control of Congress, Americans can expect safer streets, lower taxes, secure borders, and energy dominance," White House spokesperson Olivia Wales told Fox News Digital. TRUMP TOUTS ‘GOLDEN AGE’ AT OHIO RALLY, URGES VOTERS TO DELIVER GOP MIDTERM WINS The demanding schedule has also produced some memorable moments aboard Air Force One. Bruesewitz recalled one particularly exhausting West Coast trip that left him sleeping aboard the presidential aircraft at 4 a.m. "I had a picture of me sleeping on the Air Force One at 4 a.m. [that] ended up somehow in the group chat of all the congressional first spouses," he recalled. The photograph drew messages from lawmakers' wives surprised by how exhausted he appeared. TRUMP WON THIS RELIABLY RED STATE BY DOUBLE DIGITS. NOW A DEADLOCKED RACE IS BRINGING HIM BACK Despite the long hours, Bruesewitz described an atmosphere reminiscent of Trump's 2024 campaign, with staffers moving from one event to the next and the president maintaining a packed schedule. And while the president remains focused on official business and preparing his remarks during flights to campaign stops, Bruesewitz said the mood aboard Air Force One shifts considerably on the way home. On return flights, staffers unwind with music and football, including a recent Green Bay Packers game that Bruesewitz, a devoted fan of the team, watched aboard the presidential aircraft. PRESIDENT TALKS 'TRUMP OCEAN,' TRADES JOKES WITH TENNESSEE CROWD AS KID ROCK KICKS OFF SPRAWLING RALLY The campaign stops have also featured appearances by high-profile celebrities, including boxing legends Mike Tyson and Evander Holyfield and rapper Nicki Minaj. Bruesewitz recalled escorting Tyson to his seat after the boxing legend arrived at an event in New York, drawing excited reactions from attendees who recognized him. SKY-HIGH GAS PRICES AREN'T SHAKING TRUMP'S MAGA FAITHFUL IN OIL COUNTRY AS SUPPORTERS WARN OF BIGGER THREAT But one of Bruesewitz's favorite moments came during a recent stop in Port Huron, Michigan, where Minaj joined Trump for an appearance that drew a packed arena despite competing with a Detroit Lions football game. Bruesewitz said the stop was particularly memorable because many attendees were seeing Trump in person for the first time. "You could see and sense the enthusiasm of the attendees in the crowd," he said. "They were excited about Nicki going, but they were also just so pumped to be able to see the president in person." TRUMP'S MAGA FAITHFUL SEND WARNING TO REPUBLICANS AHEAD OF HIGH-STAKES MIDTERM ELECTIONS The final stretch also brought a late shift in Trump's campaign schedule, with in-person stops in Kansas and Iowa reinstated for Sunday after initially being scrapped in favor of tele-rallies aimed at reaching voters across nearly 20 states. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP After weeks of travel, packed arenas and a demanding schedule aboard Air Force One, Trump's campaign operation is set to close Monday with an appearance at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and a rapid-fire series of tele-rallies as Republicans make their final appeal to voters ahead of Election Day.

articles.title: Poll flashes warning signs for Republicans in 7 battleground Senate races
articles.summary: Senate polls show Democrats leading in Texas, Kansas, Ohio, Maine and Alaska, with Trump's approval at just 38% across the seven battlegrounds.
articles.body: Republicans are trailing Democrats in seven key Senate battlegrounds, including longtime GOP strongholds Texas and Kansas, according to a poll released Sunday, just days before the midterm elections. The New York Times/Siena poll found Democratic candidates leading in five states currently represented by Republican senators — Alaska, Kansas, Maine, Ohio and Texas — while the race in Iowa is virtually tied. In Michigan, the only Democratic-held Senate seat surveyed, the party's candidate holds a double-digit lead. Don Levy, executive director of the Siena Research Institute, said the results suggest Democrats could capture control of the Senate, though he cautioned that several races remain within the poll's margin of error. SENATE CONTROL IS A COIN FLIP — AND DEMOCRATS’ PATH RUNS THROUGH TRUMP COUNTRY "While a blue wave and Democratic control of the Senate is, according to our polls, a distinct possibility, with so many races within the poll's total margin of error, a Senate majority for either party remains possible," Levy said. The findings are particularly striking in Texas, which has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1988, and Kansas, where Democrats have not won a Senate race since 1932. In Texas, Democratic state lawmaker James Talarico leads Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton 50% to 43% among likely voters. In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton leads Republican Sen. Roger Marshall 49% to 44%. The poll also found former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown leading Republican Sen. Jon Husted in Ohio, 49% to 44%, while Democrat Troy Jackson leads Republican Sen. Susan Collins in Maine, 51% to 45%. In Alaska, former Democratic Rep. Mary Peltola leads Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan 48% to 46%. Iowa is even closer, with Democrat Josh Turek edging Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson 48% to 47%. In Michigan, Democrat Abdul El-Sayed holds the largest lead of the seven Senate races surveyed, leading Republican Mike Rogers 53% to 42%. The poll also found signs of broader dissatisfaction with President Donald Trump and Republicans' handling of the economy. Just 38% of likely voters across the seven states approve of Trump's job performance, according to the Times, despite Trump carrying five of those states by double-digit margins in the 2024 presidential election. Democrats hold a nine-point advantage over Republicans on which party voters trust more to address the cost of living, with Democratic Senate candidates leading on the issue in all seven states. The poll also found Democratic candidates leading among independent voters in every state surveyed. VETERAN DEM OPERATIVE SAYS SUBPAR GOP CANDIDATES POISED TO HAND OVER SENATE MAJORITY Democratic candidates improved their standing in six of the seven states compared with Times/Siena polls conducted in September. Alaska was the lone exception. Still, the poll offered some encouraging signs for Republicans. Voters who made their decisions within the past month favored Republican candidates by nine points, and several races remain within the margin of error. The Times also noted that polling underestimated Collins in 2020, when she trailed in every survey before winning re-election comfortably. Democrats must defend their existing Senate seats and flip at least four Republican-held seats to capture control of the chamber. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The surveys of likely voters were conducted from Oct. 23 through Nov. 1, with state-level margins of sampling error ranging from plus or minus 3.4 percentage points in Texas to 5 percentage points in Alaska.

articles.title: Trump plans to deliver closing message at Reflecting Pool
articles.summary: President Trump will make his final pitch to voters Monday ahead of Election Day at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, using the Washington landmark to tout his administration’s beautification projects in the nation’s capital. Trump’s remarks will focus on the agenda he and Republican lawmakers have advanced since the start of his second term, a…
articles.body:
President Trump will make his final pitch to voters Monday ahead of Election Day at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool , using the Washington landmark to tout his administration’s beautification projects in the nation’s capital.

Trump’s remarks will focus on the agenda he and Republican lawmakers have advanced since the start of his second term, a source familiar told NewsNation. The president is also expected to promote his expensive and controversial restoration projects, including the pool’s expensive renovation that had a list of issues .

The White House confirmed the event Sunday, hours after Trump floated the possibility while speaking to reporters in Iowa.

“We might hold it tomorrow or something,” the president said, adding that an appearance at the landmark would “show how beautiful it is.”

The expected speech marks an unconventional end to Trump’s midterm campaign blitz , with the president opting to spend the final day before the election in Washington instead of rallying in a battleground state to boost GOP voter turnout.

Trump has held more than 25 rallies over the past month in an effort to help Republicans maintain control of the House and Senate amid a record-low approval rating and voter frustration over the war in Iran, rising energy prices and the economy.

The decision to visit the Reflecting Pool for the speech also puts renewed attention on a renovation project that has been plagued by delays, ballooning costs and legal controversies over alleged vandalism .

The pool’s renovation is part of Trump’s broader push to reshape the nation’s capital during his second term. His administration also demolished the White House’s East Wing to make room for a new ballroom, transformed the Rose Garden into a patio and pursued other construction projects around the federal district.

articles.title: Reject the oath-breakers and election-deniers on the ballot tomorrow
articles.summary: Hundreds of candidates on this year’s ballots are undermining confidence in elections, despite repeated findings that the electoral process is fair.
articles.body:
Around 250 million Americans are eligible to vote in tomorrow’s midterm elections. By the end of last week, more than 34 million already had. And all the while, President Trump and his allies are doing all they can to meddle in the process.

Voters will find that hundreds of candidates on this year’s ballots are undermining confidence in elections, despite repeated findings that the electoral process is fair. Many participated in Trump’s plot to overturn the 2020 election . Others have simply bought into his persistent but entirely unsubstantiated claims of election fraud . Either way, voters should reject them.

No responsibility of citizenship is more important than choosing who represents us in government. In democracies, it is a sacred secular ritual. It gives every eligible citizen a measure of political power, including the ability to stand against tyranny and corruption, influence how tax dollars are spent, and help shape the country’s future.

Fair elections allow power to transfer peacefully from one set of leaders to the next. Scholars call this a “ rare and recent practice ” among nations. Its upkeep is one reason every public official in the U.S. must swear to protect and defend the Constitution.

Trump has taken that oath twice, but he has repeatedly violated it as president. He is now openly engaged in a conspiracy to erode voter confidence in elections and interfere with the ability of states to run them honestly . His interference is unpatriotic, unethical and unconstitutional.

Trump has engaged the U.S. Departments of Justice and Homeland Security in this effort. They are not acting alone. According to an Oct. 5 analysis by the nonpartisan States United Democracy Center, voters will find the names of 197 election deniers across 43 states on their midterm ballots. The center defines election denial as candidates who helped spread Trump’s persistent lies about the 2020 election, refused to certify the results on Jan. 6, 2021, or tried to overturn former President Joe Biden’s victory.

States United counts 163 congressional races with election deniers on the ballot. That is significant, because those elected to the House or Senate will participate in certifying the 2028 presidential election, the process that Trump and his co-conspirators tried to sabotage in 2021 by appointing false electors and inciting the riot that delayed Congress’s validation of Joe Biden’s lawful victory.

At least 33 other deniers across 21 states are running for statewide offices, States United says, hoping to become governors, attorneys general or secretaries of state, the chief election officers in most states.

Three Republican gubernatorial candidates on tomorrow’s ballots are departing members of Congress that the center has identified as election deniers: Reps. Andy Biggs (R-Ariz.), Byron Donalds (R-Fla), and Tom Tiffany (R-Wis). They voted to sustain objections to valid electoral votes during the 2021 certification process.

These candidates should be defeated because their involvement affronts the democratic process. Study after study has concluded that claims of significant election irregularities, such as voter fraud, are baseless.

“American elections are quite well-run,” states the American Bar Association. “[E]fforts to cast doubt on their security and accuracy pose a grave systemic threat to our form of government.”

Interestingly, some legal scholars argue the Constitution disqualifies members of the denial movement from holding any public office. Section 3 of the 14th Amendment says that any federal or state official who swears to uphold the Constitution (all public officials are obligated to do so) and then participates in or supports a rebellion against it should be disqualified from serving in office again.

But in 2024, the U.S. Supreme Court muddied the waters on how to enforce this. In a 5-4 ruling, the court said only Congress can disqualify federal officials for rebellion. The Constitution doesn’t say that.

Although Trump won’t be on tomorrow’s ballots, voters can hold him accountable by rejecting the midterm candidates who participated in denying the 2020 election outcome and who continue supporting his efforts to rig the electoral process , intimidate state election officials , destroy public confidence in voting, and interfere with states’ constitutional election duties.

Facts are facts. The moneychangers, snake-oil salesmen, charlatans, crooks, capitulators, collaborators and cowards have taken over the temples of democracy. They plan to stay. Tomorrow, we must begin kicking them out.

William S. Becker is co-editor of and a contributor to “Democracy Unchained: How to Rebuild Government for the People,” and a contributor to “Democracy in a Hotter Time.” He previously served as a senior official in the Wisconsin Department of Justice. He is currently executive director of the Presidential Climate Action Project.

articles.title: Steve Hilton rallies at 'symbol of 16 years of Democrat failure' in closing days of California race
articles.summary: Steve Hilton rallied in Pacific Palisades, calling the wildfire devastation a symbol of 16 years of Democratic failure ahead of Tuesday's election.
articles.body: Republican California gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton rallied Sunday in Pacific Palisades, a Los Angeles neighborhood devastated by the January 2025 wildfires, blaming Democratic leadership for the destruction and slow recovery just days before voters will choose the state's next governor. "I’m so sorry. And it’s so sad about what happened because it could and should have been avoided," Hilton told supporters and residents. "This place is a symbol of 16 years of Democrat failure." The Palisades Fire burned more than 23,000 acres and destroyed roughly 6,800 structures, many of them homes. Fueled by powerful winds and dry conditions, the blaze displaced tens of thousands of residents and devastated large sections of the community, leaving a massive rebuilding effort in its wake. JURY DEADLOCKS IN FEDERAL TRIAL OF MAN ACCUSED OF STARTING DEADLY PALISADES FIRE IN LOS ANGELES Hilton argued that the disaster and its aftermath reflected broader failures of California's Democratic leadership, from wildfire prevention and emergency response to rebuilding efforts. "These are not random, disconnected events," Hilton said. "These are what has gone wrong in the state of California over 16 years of one-party rule." Democrats have held California's governorship for the past 16 years. Hilton faces Democrat Xavier Becerra, a former state attorney general and Health and Human Services secretary under President Joe Biden, in Tuesday's election to succeed term-limited Gov. Gavin Newsom. Hilton, a former Fox News commentator who previously advised British Prime Minister David Cameron, has made criticism of the state's Democratic leadership a central theme of his campaign. STEVE HILTON LAUNCHES AD MOCKING XAVIER BECERRA'S '36 YEARS' AS A CAREER POLITICIAN IN CALIFORNIA GOV RACE At the rally, he accused state and local officials of failing to adequately prepare for the fires and help residents rebuild, blaming what he called a combination of "incompetence, ideology and corruption." He also criticized environmental and land-management policies, arguing that inadequate brush clearance contributed to the destruction. "The ideology that for years and years and years not just failed to clear the brush that could have prevented these fires here and in Altadena ... but deliberately chose not to do that," Hilton said. Hilton pledged to appoint a recovery CEO to oversee rebuilding efforts if elected, arguing that residents had waited too long for their communities to recover. "I spent the time, I’ve listened, and I can tell you right now, when I’m governor, I will appoint a recovery CEO to finally get things done, to finally get what you deserve," Hilton said. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP He closed by urging voters to reject the idea that California must remain under Democratic control. "This is not a blue state. It is not a red state. It’s the Golden State," Hilton said. "And we are going to fight with everything we’ve got."

articles.title: Midterms: The key US Senate races to watch
articles.summary: All eyes are on a handful of Senate races that will decide control of the prized upper chamber. Here's a quick guide.
articles.body:
Millions of Americans are about to decide the future of the Republican-controlled Congress in a midterm election that will have a significant impact on President Donald Trump's final two years in office.

All eyes are on a handful of Senate races that will decide control of the prized upper chamber.

A four-seat gain by Democrats would give them control - and with it the power to limit Trump's ambitions, reject his judicial nominations and investigate his administration.

Billions of dollars are being poured into the 35 races across the country, but only a handful could go either way.

There are seven Senate races deemed to be a toss-up by independent elections analyst Cook Political Report .

Here, we profile the personalities making waves in these much-watched contests.

This race has been marred by controversy over the appearance of a second candidate named Dan Sullivan on the ballot. The Republican senator of that name faces stiff competition from Mary Peltola and accuses her of introducing his namesake to confuse voters, which she denies.

The race may ultimately be the tipping point state that decides which party controls the chamber if, as expected, Alaska is one of the slower states to reach an outcome.

Peltola, a former House member and the first Alaska Native to be elected to Congress, has run on a platform of "fish, family, freedom" and has attacked Sullivan's record as Alaska's natural resources commissioner.

Two-term senator Sullivan, a long-time Marine Corps reservist who also served as Alaska's attorney general, has accused Peltola's campaign of links to an effort to confuse Republican voters which led to a second man named Dan Sullivan entering the race.

The Peltola campaign denies any such link, though the issue is the subject of a state investigation and a justice department lawsuit, which on Sunday was rejected by a judge.

Alaska's ranked-choice system also adds uncertainty to the mix, and the state has historically been difficult to poll, with surveys historically underestimating Republican voters.

Sullivan, 61, only retired from the US Marines as recently as 2024, after a 30-year career that included deployments in to Afghanistan and the Middle East. Peltola, 53, grew up fishing salmon with her father, later becoming the first person born in the state to actually represent it in Congress.

One of the few Republican senators who voted to convict Trump when he was impeached in 2021, Susan Collins has consistently outperformed her party in this Democratic-leaning state, partly by presenting herself as a rebel. Her opponent Troy Jackson, who draws on his background as a lumberjack to persuade blue-collar Mainers he can relate to them, hopes that time is finally running out for one of the survivors of US politics.

Collins is hoping her reputation as a centrist will persuade independent-minded voters in a state that reliably votes Democratic in presidential elections.

Now her campaign will test whether Republicans can win by distancing themselves from Trump.

Collins, who is seeking her sixth term, entered the midterm cycle as one of the most vulnerable incumbent Republicans seeking re-election.

But she has been helped by controversy on the other side of the aisle involving Graham Platner, who was ultimately replaced as the Democratic nominee by Jackson, a former president of the Maine state senate.

Both Jackson and Collins oppose Trump's tariffs on Canada, mindful of the impact they are having on this border state. Unlike Collins, though, he favours the abolition of the US Immigration and Customs Enforcement agency (ICE).

Collins, 73, began her political career fresh from college in the 1970s and she entered the US Senate in 1997. Jackson, 58, is a logger who became politically active when he helped to lead a protest to block lower-paid workers from Canada entering Maine.

James Talarico aims to end a decades-long electoral drought for the Democrats in Texas - and show that one of the Republicans' main strongholds could be in play for the 2028 presidential election. His match-up with Ken Paxton has become the most expensive Senate race ever.

Republican Paxton knows his party has been winning statewide races in Texas for more than 30 years.

Texas State Representative James Talarico, a former schoolteacher and Presbyterian seminary student, is the latest Democrat hoping to break his party's long losing streak.

Texas Republicans are facing a daunting combination of headwinds. It is a challenging national political environment for conservatives and there are several state issues like data centre construction and aggressive immigration enforcement that have cut against their party. Added to that is a controversial candidate, Paxton.

The campaign has been acrimonious, with Talarico targeting Paxton's 2023 impeachment by the Republican-controlled state House of Representatives for alleged corruption, bribery and abuse of power. Paxton denied the charges and was later acquitted by the state Senate, calling the impeachment a "politically motivated sham from the beginning".

Supported by more than $170m in funds from tech mogul Elon Musk, Paxton has attempted to paint Talarico as a liberal who is out of touch with Texans on issues like transgender rights, law enforcement, immigration and energy policy.

A Democratic victory here might indicate America's second-biggest electoral prize in a presidential election could be within their reach in 2028 - a notion that could dramatically reshape the nation's political landscape.

Before he entered public service, Paxton spent 14 years launching and building his own law firm. He served in the state House and Senate before becoming the chief legal officer in Texas.

Talarico taught at a middle school in San Antonio, in a neighbourhood he has described as one of the poorest in the state. He has studied theology and names Pope Leo as a "spiritual hero".

This is one of the most bitter contests, with left-wing candidate Abdul El-Sayed aiming to keep this crucial seat in Democratic hands. He is up against Mike Rogers, a Republican former FBI agent who received a surprise endorsement from El-Sayed's defeated Democratic rival, only adding to the acrimony that has characterised this race from the start.

A doctor and public health official, El-Sayed is one of the most left-wing Senate nominees this election cycle.

He supports a government-run health insurance system and the abolition of ICE. His strong criticism of Israel has been a source of tension in the party.

Rogers, who emphasises his military and intelligence background, has managed to maintain Trump's support despite decrying his Canada tariffs and his Russia diesel deal.

He has also diverged from the president by calling for a quick end to the war with Iran. El-Sayed would be the first Muslim person ever elected to the US Senate.

As well as attacking him for his politics, Trump and Rogers have sought to link him to the Muslim Brotherhood; El-Sayed has denounced the organisation.

The president has also invoked 9/11 and even called him a "jihadist" without citing any evidence, prompting a backlash and accusations of Islamophobia.

El-Sayed, 41, was born and raised in Michigan before his medical studies in the US and UK and subsequent work in the sector. Rogers, 63, served in the US Army and in the FBI before entering Congress and emerging as a key advocate of US surveillance policies.

Trump made the trip to Iowa on his final day of campaign rallies, such is its importance. Polls have it as a toss-up between Republican and former TV news host Ashley Hinson and Democrat Josh Turek, who won gold at basketball at two Paralympic Games.

Farms, tariffs and Trump have all emerged as key issues in the closely-watched race.

Hinson has slightly distanced herself from the president, urging him to end the war with Iran and breaking with him on easing beef tariffs, while at the same time defending Trump's broader tariff policies as important.

Meanwhile, Turek argues that Trump's tariffs have led to "farmageddon" in the largely rural state. He has also sought to convince voters that the war in Iran has led to rising fuel and fertiliser costs.

Hinson has cast Turek as a candidate who would vote as an "East Coast liberal".

The two have also clashed on issues ranging from taxes and social security to immigration. The last time a Democrat won a federal election in Iowa was nearly 20 years ago.

Hinson, 43, is a former local news reporter who says her journalistic background helps her understand the issues faced by the state's farmers and small businesses. Turek, 47, was born with spina bifida, going through multiple surgeries before representing the USA at wheelchair basketball at four Paralympic Games, twice triumphantly.

A Democratic victory in Kansas would upend 94 years of history - the last time this Midwestern state elected a Democratic senator was 1932. Senator Roger Marshall is the Republican trying to avoid a humbling defeat, while first-time candidate and Methodist pastor Adam Hamilton is the Democrat trying to break records.

Marshall has closely aligned himself as a Trump-aligned, pro-farmer candidate.

Hamilton, who once considered running as an independent, has pitched himself as a candidate that can bridge the partisan divide. He has largely campaigned on a message of lower costs and protecting healthcare access.

Marshall has sought to attack Hamilton's record as a pastor, describing him as "too woke" for the conservative state.

Marshall, meanwhile, has been under scrutiny ever since reports emerged that he sued patients unable to pay their medical bills. He told Fox News the story was a hit job by the left media and senior Democrats.

The tight race is broadly seen as a potentially ominous sign for Republicans.

A Hamilton victory would be seen as a sign of increasing dissatisfaction with Trump's policies - particularly on economics - in territory that was once considered safe for the party.

Both Marshall, 66, and Hamilton, 62, highlight that they are fifth-generation Kansans who are in close touch with local issues. Marshall worked for 25 years as an obstetrician, delivering some 5,000 babies, while his rival Hamilton founded a church which became the centre of the largest United Methodist congregation in America.

Trump won this state with ease in 2024 and no-one a year ago considered it in play for the midterms. But Republican Senator Jon Husted finds himself neck and neck with Democrat Sherrod Brown who is running to get his old job back, having represented Ohio in the Senate for many years before losing his seat.

Husted was appointed in 2025 to the Senate seat vacated by Vice-President JD Vance, and is now running to serve the rest of Vance's term.

He promises to use his business experience to bring jobs and growth to Ohio.

In a different election cycle he would probably be the favourite to win this onetime swing state that has become reliably red in the Trump era.

But Husted is facing a formidable challenge from Brown, who has high name recognition from three decades representing Ohio in Congress.

Brown is known as a champion of workers and was advocating economic populist policies long before others in his party.

The race is a referendum on Trump's economic policies, in particular his trade wars that have impacted the manufacturing and auto industries that underpin Ohio's economy.

Husted, 59, began life in a foster home and was in the world of business before politics; he was an elite American football player at college and his physique has been repeatedly praised by President Trump at rallies. Brown, 73, was introduced to political activism from a young age and was recruited into local politics even before graduating from Yale.

By Bernd Debusmann, Daniel Bush and Anthony Zurcher in Washington, and James FitzGerald and Tom Geoghegan in London.
