articles.title: LEE CARTER: The 5 words that explain this election better than any commercial
articles.summary: Affordability, socialism, corruption, Trump and turnout: five words a researcher says explain the 2026 midterms better than $11 billion in ads.
articles.body: Eleven billion dollars. Actually, more than that. Political advertising spending and reservations have now exceeded $11.6 billion, making this the most expensive election cycle for political advertising in American history. For that kind of money, you'd think somebody might have figured out how to make groceries cheaper. MIDTERMS UNLEASH WHAT MAY BE THE NASTIEST BARRAGE OF ATTACK ADS YET Instead, Americans have endured months of attack ads, apocalyptic warnings and politicians insisting that civilization itself is on the ballot. Again. As a researcher, I've spent much of this year studying what Americans believe, what frustrates them and, perhaps most importantly, what might motivate them to vote. And I've become convinced that five words explain this election better than a thousand campaign commercials. Affordability. Socialism. Corruption. Trump. Turnout. Each tells us something about the American electorate. Together, they reveal something neither party should find particularly comforting. Americans may be less interested in voting for somebody than in voting against something. INDEPENDENT VOTERS AREN’T PICKING A POLITICAL TEAM, THEY JUST FEEL PICKED ON And the two parties are betting on very different fears. AFFORDABILITY Washington has a remarkable talent for telling Americans how well they're doing while Americans are busy wondering how they're going to pay for everything. Inflation is cooling! The stock market is booming! Economic growth is strong! Wonderful. Now explain why a family of four needs a financing plan to buy groceries and a second job to take everyone to Disney World. Here's what politicians keep missing: Americans don't experience the economy as a collection of statistics. They experience it as a series of small humiliations. FOX NEWS POLL: SQUEEZED BY COSTS, FRUSTRATED VOTERS TURN TO THE DEMOCRATS Putting something back on the grocery shelf. Declining a dinner invitation. Explaining to your child why the family vacation will have to wait another year. The economy isn't what Washington says is happening. It's what Americans can afford to do. Republicans have spent much of this campaign telling voters that things are getting better. Democrats have spent it reminding them how expensive everything remains. The Democrats have the easier argument. But there's a catch. Convincing voters that Republicans haven't made their lives better is not the same as convincing them that Democrats will. One requires an attack ad. The other requires an actual plan. SOCIALISM For years, Republicans have warned that Democrats are taking America toward socialism. The accusation has been deployed so enthusiastically that you'd think Karl Marx was running for Congress in every competitive district. Democrats often dismiss it as tired political fearmongering. They may be making a serious mistake. In polling I've been examining, the share of Republicans energized to vote against socialism has climbed from 50% to 59% in just a month. Think about what that means. Republicans can be disappointed in their candidates, frustrated with the economy and unhappy with their party's performance while remaining extraordinarily motivated to vote. Why? Because they may believe the alternative is worse. Disappointment makes people complain. Fear makes them act. Democrats see socialism as an outdated Republican talking point. Many Republicans see it as a threat to the country they love. That doesn't mean Republicans are necessarily happy with their own party. It means they may be willing to vote for a party they don't particularly like to stop one they fear even more. And that's a potentially powerful turnout strategy hiding in plain sight. CORRUPTION Remember when draining the swamp was a campaign promise? Apparently, the swamp has become a bipartisan swimming pool. According to research from the Brennan Center and Wesleyan Media Project, nearly one-third of congressional television ads this cycle have referenced government ethics or campaign finance. Americans increasingly suspect that the people running the country are playing by an entirely different set of rules. Democrats have eagerly made corruption a central attack against Republicans. But they should be careful about throwing stones from inside their own rather expensive glass houses. Consider Alaska, where reports that Democratic-aligned operatives helped recruit a second candidate named Dan Sullivan have sparked allegations of election manipulation. Democrat Mary Peltola has denied knowing about the effort. Whatever the ultimate findings, the controversy is a reminder that political hardball doesn't have a party registration. But there's something deeper happening here. When Americans are working harder and getting less while politicians and well-connected insiders somehow keep getting richer, every economic frustration begins to look like evidence of a rigged system. The grocery bill isn't simply too high. Someone must be benefiting. Healthcare isn't simply too expensive. Someone must be gaming the system. You can convince voters that your opponent is corrupt without convincing them that you're honest. And when voters believe everybody is playing dirty, the winner may inherit the office without inheriting much public confidence. TRUMP Donald Trump isn't running for Congress. You'd never know it. He's crisscrossing the country, dominating headlines and rallying supporters as though his own name were printed at the top of every ballot. And he may understand something that the conventional election narrative is missing. Trump's national approval ratings are weak. His base, however, remains intensely loyal. Those aren't contradictory facts. They're the defining feature of his political appeal. Democrats have spent more than $163 million on advertising mentioning Trump since September 1, compared with roughly $11 million by Republicans. Apparently, the Democratic Party's most valuable campaign surrogate is the Republican president. But Trump has an advantage of his own. Many of his supporters aren't Republicans who happen to like Trump. They're Trump supporters who happen to vote Republican. And those voters don't always show up when he isn't running. Which may explain why he's campaigning as though he is. His supporters may not feel particularly inspired to save the Republican Party. But they might be motivated to save Donald Trump from a Democratic Congress. Democrats want this election to be a referendum on Trump. Trump wants it to be a referendum on whether his supporters will defend him. Both sides are making the same man the center of the election. They're just hoping voters respond in opposite ways. TURNOUT And that brings us to the word that could determine everything. Turnout. The polls tell a remarkably consistent story. Democrats have an advantage. Economic frustration is widespread. The president is unpopular. But elections aren't simply a measure of public opinion. They're a measure of who participates. As a researcher, I believe deeply in what polling can tell us. We can measure attitudes, identify motivations and model which voters are likely to show up. But there's a reason we call them likely voters. The most consequential difference in an election isn't always between Republicans and Democrats. It's between people who are angry enough to vote and people who are exhausted enough to stay home. Democrats are angry about what Republicans have done. Republicans may be frightened by what they believe Democrats will do. Independents may be frustrated with both. And that creates a fascinating question. Which emotion will actually get people out of the house? Gallup recently found that 56% of Americans have given considerable thought to this election, a record for this point in a midterm cycle. But paying attention and participating aren't the same thing. A wave of Democratic enthusiasm in safely blue districts won't change control of Congress. A smaller Republican surge in a handful of competitive races could. And a relatively modest number of independents deciding to stay home or to show up could rewrite the headlines. The polls can tell us where voters stand. Tuesday will tell us which voters stand up. And that distinction could determine the election. Here's what I suspect both parties will get wrong once the votes are counted. If Democrats win big, they'll declare that America has rejected Trumpism and embraced their vision. If Republicans outperform expectations, they'll insist voters have reaffirmed the president's agenda. Both may be mistaking a victory for an endorsement. Voters can fire one party without falling in love with the other. And they can stick with a party they don't particularly like because they're more afraid of the alternative. That's the paradox of American politics in 2026. We have two parties desperately trying to win an election in a country increasingly skeptical that either deserves to. After more than $11 billion in political advertising, thousands of polls and enough promises to wallpaper the Capitol, Americans may be sending a remarkably simple message. They don't want politicians to win another argument. They want someone to make their lives better. Tuesday will tell us who wins power. articles.title: Donald Trump se enfrenta a las elecciones al Congreso de Estados Unidos y los expertos lo sentencian: "Disfuncional y autoritario"
articles.standfirst: El descontento económico y las decisiones estratégicas amenazan la estabilidad del Partido Republicano
articles.summary: El descontento económico y las decisiones estratégicas amenazan la estabilidad del Partido Republicano
articles.body: Las elecciones de mitad de mandato de 2026 se perfilan como un momento decisivo para el panorama político de Estados Unidos. Aunque las dinámicas electorales responden habitualmente a múltiples factores, la coyuntura actual presenta condicionantes particulares. Charles Lane, analista político en el Washington Post, es claro: "El Partido Republicano corre el riesgo de una derrota total, esencialmente por una sola razón: el gobierno disfuncional y autoritario del presidente Donald Trump, tanto del gobierno como de su partido". A comienzos de año, la posición del partido parecía sólida, respaldada por indicadores económicos estables y el control estratégico de contiendas clave en el Senado. Sin embargo, las fricciones geopolíticas y el aumento vertiginoso de los costos energéticos tras la escalada de tensiones en Oriente Medio modificaron la percepción ciudadana. A esta situación se sumó la reactivación de una agenda comercial restrictiva mediante aranceles a la importación, lo que afectó directamente a sectores productivos rurales e industriales. En este contexto, Lane señala que "Hasta aquí llegó el supuesto fin de la “Bideninflación”", visibilizando el desgaste de la narrativa económica del partido. En el ámbito interno, la selección de candidatos para las primarias desencadenó disputas severas. La sustitución de perfiles competitivos y tradicionales por perfiles alineados de manera estricta con el ejecutivo provocó fracturas en plazas históricamente seguras como Carolina del Norte, Texas y Georgia. Evaluando este proceso de nominación, Lane afirma que "Desde que Calígula intentó nombrar a su caballo cónsul, ningún líder había elegido de forma tan imprudente". Asimismo, el autor subraya la dinámica de lealtades políticas al remarcar cómo Ken Paxton era considerado un político en medio de controversias pero plenamente "leal", lo que condicionó los resultados en el terreno electoral. La tensión se extendió a la gestión de la seguridad interior y a los incidentes derivados de operativos migratorios con el ICE, los cuales minaron el respaldo en sectores demográficos estratégicos, como el electorado latino. A su vez, los desatinos comunicativos en mítines y la impopularidad de proyectos de infraestructura aumentaron la ventaja de la oposición en las proyecciones para la Cámara de Representantes y el Senado. Ante este escenario, la responsabilidad no recae de forma exclusiva en el liderazgo del ejecutivo, sino también en la estructura legislativa que respaldó cada medida sin ejercer un contrapeso efectivo. El desenlace de las elecciones determinará la reconfiguración del Congreso y el alcance del poder ejecutivo en los próximos años. La falta de contención a políticas erráticas ha dejado al descubierto las vulnerabilidades de un partido que cedió su autonomía organizativa. Al analizar el trasfondo de esta crisis institucional y el papel de las bases parlamentarias, Lane concluye de forma contundente: "Pocas veces un líder político ha demostrado un desprecio tan temerario por los intereses de sus seguidores. Pocas veces sus seguidores se lo han merecido más".

articles.title: James Carville makes crude remark about Haley Stevens over shocking Rogers endorsement
articles.summary: James Carville compared Haley Stevens to a "used condom" after she endorsed Mike Rogers, but one critic says his outrage is inconsistent with his prior comments.
articles.body: Democratic strategist James Carville compared Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., to a "used condom" on the "Politicon" podcast Sunday, hours after she endorsed Republican Mike Rogers. "I mean, lady, if you're going to sell your soul, you got to get more for it than a f---ing cheeseburger, OK," Carville said. "I'm just telling you that you got to put some kind of a price on yourself for some kind of a g------ self-pride, but your political career is over." Carville said Stevens' endorsement of Rogers would leave her without support from either party, using a vulgar comparison to describe how he believed Republicans and Democrats viewed her. "If you think that these Republicans are going to treat you as anything other than what they view you as, and that is, let me just break the news to you, a used condom. The Democrats don't even think you're worth a used condom. But that's about where you are," he continued. "You made your bed, sleep in it. You s--- in your mess kit, eat it." EL SAYED'S LEFT-WING ALLIES ATTACK 'EVIL' STEVENS AFTER BOMBSHELL ROGERS ENDORSEMENT Stephen Kent, media director at the Consumer Choice Center, told Fox News Digital that Carville's criticism conflicted with his recent willingness to contemplate Republican victories to limit the influence of democratic socialists. "Putting aside the gross language, this is ridiculous coming from a guy who just two weeks ago said he'd prefer Republicans hold on to a handful of House seats so that the Democratic Socialist bloc doesn't have too much control of the chamber," Kent said. "He said after this election, he didn't want to be in the same party as Hasan Piker. So for him to chide Haley Stevens for making the exact same calculus is not shrewd — it's just hypocrisy," he added. Kent was referring to Carville's recent comments, where the Democratic strategist said he'd rather Republicans win by five seats in the House of Representatives in the midterm elections than Democrats winning by the same number — out of concerns the Democratic Party would become "hostages" to the Democratic Socialists of America. HASAN PIKER'S INFLUENCE TESTS BREAKING POINT OF DEMOCRATIC PARTY Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers on Sunday after Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed disinvited her from a planned unity event amid a dispute over an advertisement from Rebellion PAC, founded by The Young Turks host Cenk Uygur. The ad linked U.S. military support for Israel to high grocery prices, prompting Stevens to call it antisemitic and demand El-Sayed condemn it. El-Sayed, who defeated Stevens in their Senate primary, said his campaign did not produce the ad and that he disagreed with its contents. Far-left streamer Hasan Piker attacked Stevens' motives in a post to X, claiming she was "weirdly obsessed with Israel." "haley stevens is not the spokesperson for democrats, she’s not the spox for jewish people or black people," Piker said on X. "she's a self interested striver who’s weirdly obsessed with israel and has been paid handsomely for this strange obsession. this race is about solving the affordability crisis, defending democracy, fighting back against the racialized violence all communities have faced since trump came into power and serving michigan. haley and mike rogers serve trump, and trump serves the epstein class. the choice is clear." "She’s clearly a disturbed, deranged, dishonest woman (less than 48 hours ago she was swearing to the NYT she was backing Abdul)," Zeteo News' editor-in-chief Mehdi Hasan also said on X, going on to attack the Democratic establishment for putting forward a "complete traitor." FORMER RIVAL DODGES FULL-THROATED EL-SAYED ENDORSEMENT AFTER BITTER SENATE PRIMARY Former DNC Vice Chair David Hogg also attacked Stevens and urged Democrats to denounce the congresswoman. "If you supported Haley Stevens now is your time to speak out, denounce her as the Republican she is and apologize for supporting a traitor," Hogg wrote. articles.title: The 2026 midterms are tomorrow and the final polls are here. Which party has a better chance of winning?
articles.summary: The latest New York Times surveys show Democrats leading key Senate races in Michigan, Texas, Kansas, Maine, Ohio, Alaska and Iowa. Could this be a "wave" el...
articles.body:
The 2026 midterm elections are tomorrow. So where do things stand — nationwide — in the race to control Congress? Which party has a better chance of, you know, winning? To get a sense of that, it helps to geek out over some cold, hard data.

The usual caveats apply, of course. Polls aren't predictions; they're momentary snapshots of public opinion. And they have been wrong before .

Yet time is almost up — and the stakes on Nov. 3 couldn't be higher, especially for President Trump, who has enjoyed complete Republican control of Congress for the first half of his second term. Flipping the House would give Democrats the power to block the president's agenda, investigate his administration and even impeach him (again); flipping the Senate would allow them to stymie his Supreme Court nominees too.

The state-by-state midterm landscape has reached its final form — and the polling trends are clear. Here are the numbers on the eve of Election Day.

Every pollster asks a version of the same question: If an election for U.S. Congress were held today, which party's candidate would you vote for in your district? In fact, this particular polling prompt is so pervasive, it's known as the "generic ballot" (at least among politics nerds).

You obviously can't divine the outcome of an entire midterm election from a single question that flattens 435 House contests into a binary choice between "the Democrat" and "the Republican." But the generic ballot can suggest which direction voters are heading.

At this point in 2022 — after nearly two years of Democratic President Joe Biden and Democratic majorities in the House and Senate — Republicans had a small but significant lead (2.5 percentage points) on the generic ballot. On Election Day, the GOP translated its final polling lead of 3 percentage points into nine seats — enough to flip the House.

At this point in 2018 — with Trump as president and Republican majorities in the House and Senate — Democrats were leading by an average of 7.3 points on the generic ballot. The next day, they picked up 41 seats and flipped the House.

Polarization wasn't as extreme in 2014 and 2010, the two midterms under Democratic President Barack Obama; minds weren't made up quite so early. But by the eve of Election Day, voters had clearly broken against Democrats. In 2014, a Republican polling lead of 2.4 points translated into a net gain of 13 seats in the House; in 2010, those numbers were 8.7 points and 63 seats, respectively.

So what does that mean for 2026? Historically speaking, a president's party almost always loses seats when voters return to the polls to judge his first two years in office. Sometimes, the backlash is so pervasive that the president's party loses pretty much every close-ish contest — a phenomenon known as a "wave" election.

Right now, Democrats have a wave-sized lead on the generic ballot — nearly 9 percentage points , on average. And that margin has held steady over the last month.

Democrats might not reprise 2018 and flip 41 House seats again in November, in part because red-state Republican lawmakers have recently redrawn congressional maps across the South to benefit their party in ways that blue-state Democrats have been unable to keep up with . But they only need to pick up three seats to win back the House.

National dynamics tend to define the composition of the incoming House. But Senate contests are quirkier — more state-specific and personality-driven. Democrats currently hold 47 Senate seats; they'd need 51 to control the chamber. (A 50-50 split would give Vice President JD Vance the tiebreaking vote). Polls suggest that flipping four Republican seats is very possible. In the states where Dems are playing defense — Michigan, Georgia, New Hampshire — their leads are solidifying; meanwhile, red states such as Iowa, Kansas, Nebraska and South Carolina seem increasingly competitive. Here are the 12 races to follow:

What the latest polls say : Jackson, who replaced Graham Platner , the Democrats' previous scandal-plagued nominee, tends to lead Collins by anywhere from 2 to 7 percentage points . The final New York Times/Siena University poll shows Jackson ahead by 6 .

Republican Mike Rogers (former member of Congress)

Democrat Abdul El-Sayed (public-health epidemiologist and former Wayne County, Mich. health director)

What the latest polls say : Eighteen polls were conducted in October. Seventeen of them showed El-Sayed in the lead, by anywhere from 1 to 9 percentage points . The final New York Times/Siena University survey gives El-Sayed an 11-point lead ; new polls from YouGov ( El-Sayed +4 ) and Research Co. ( El-Sayed +2 ) show smaller margins for the Democrat.

What the latest polls say : Brown has edged Husted in nearly every poll conducted since the first week of October, with margins ranging from 2 to 6 percentage points. The final New York Times/Siena University survey gives Brown a 6-point advantage .

Republican Mike Collins (member of Congress)

What the latest polls say : Ossoff holds a solid lead over Collins, with October polls putting him ahead by an average of 9 percentage points . A new Echelon Insights survey gives Ossoff a 15-point lead .

Republican Michael Whatley (former Republican National Committee chairman)

What the latest polls say : Cooper leads by nearly 11 points, on average . Final polls from YouGov and East Carolina University show him ahead by 11 points and 9 points, respectively.

Republican John E. Sununu (former U.S. senator)

Democrat Chris Pappas (four-term U.S. representative)

What the latest polls say : Pappas and Sununu were previously trading leads in polls in the race to replace retiring Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. But Pappas appears to have opened a substantial lead — average margin: 7.5 percentage points — over the last month. The final University of New Hampshire survey shows him ahead by 12 .

Democrat Mary Peltola (former member of Congress)

What the latest polls say : Surveys conducted in October show Peltola leading by anywhere from 2 to 7 percentage points . The final New York Times/Siena Universty poll gives her a narrow 48-46% advantage .

Republican Ashley Hinson (member of Congress)

Democrat Josh Turek (state legislator and former Paralympic athlete)

What the latest polls say : Hinson and Turek have traded small leads in surveys released since Iowa's June 2 primaries . The final YouGov and New York Times/Siena University polls show Turek ahead by 1 point; GrayHouse and co/efficient polls show Hinson leading by 2.

Republican Ken Paxton (state attorney general)

Democrat James Talarico (state legislator)

What the latest polls say : Nearly every poll conducted this fall has shown Talarico leading Paxton, though the margins were small — between 2 and 6 points. But the Democrat seems to be closing strong: final polls from Atlas Intel and the New York Times/Siena University show him ahead by 6 and 7 points, respectively.

Republican Pete Ricketts (incumbent and former governor)

Independent Dan Osborn (veteran and former union leader with Democratic support)

What the latest polls say : Surveys are few and far between. But the most recent nonpartisan results suggest Osborn could be competitive, and a couple of Osborn-affiliated polls show Ricketts and his independent challenger trading small leads. An Echelon Insights poll released on Tuesday shows Ricketts ahead by 1 point; a New York Times/Siena University survey released on Saturday gives Ricketts a 6-point lead.

Democrat Adam Hamilton (Methodist pastor who previously considered an independent run)

What the latest polls say : Only one survey conducted over the last month shows Marshall ahead (by a single point). The rest (save one tie) give Hamilton a slight edge (between 1 and 5 percentage points). A new CNN poll has Hamilton up by 4 ; a new Emerson College survey puts him ahead by roughly the same amount . On Friday, the Washington Post released a poll showing Hamilton lapping Marshall by about 10 points. But the paper questioned its own results , noting that Republicans responded at much lower rates than Democrats. The final New York Times/Siena University survey shows Hamilton ahead by 5 .

Republican Darline Graham (incumbent, appointed to replace her brother Lindsey Graham after his death in July)

Democrat Annie Andrews (pediatrician and former U.S. House candidate)

What the latest polls say : Graham held a narrow lead in most fall surveys . But it was small enough — between 1 and 3 percentage points — that Democrats are now targeting South Carolina as well. A partisan poll released on Friday gave Andrews a 5-point advantage; a new New York Times/Siena University poll shows the two candidates essentially tied.

Advantage? Democrats. They've been consistently gaining ground over the last month, to the point where they are now favored to flip the Senate — unless the polls are wrong.

Trump's approval rating — especially on affordability

To one degree or another, midterm elections are always referendums on how the president is performing. So Trump is the final piece of the puzzle.

At the moment, that's unfortunate news for Republicans on Capitol Hill and those looking to join them.

According to the data journalists at Silver Bulletin , 59.4% of Americans, on average, currently disapprove of how Trump is handling his job vs. 38% who approve. That puts the president's net approval rating at -21.5% — near his all-time low.

Here's a sampling of Trump's latest net approval numbers from a few top pollsters:

Again, history can provide perspective . In late-October 2018, Trump was about 10 points "underwater"; Republicans went on to lose 41 seats that November.

According to the New York Times , Trump has the second lowest approval rating heading into the midterms since 1946, behind only Harry Truman. George W. Bush's approval rating was higher at this point in 2006 — a year in which Democrats went on to flip the House and Senate.

Trump is earning even lower marks on voters' top 2026 issue: the cost of living . Shortly after he returned to office, roughly equal numbers of Americans approved and disapproved of how the president was handling inflation. But today, 70% disapprove and 25% approve. That's a 45-point gap.

In comparison, Biden's approval rating on inflation was rarely underwater by more than 30 points during his presidency — a period that coincided with the economic shocks of COVID-19 and ended with him choosing not to stand for reelection.

articles.title: Haley Stevens' endorsement stunt backfires with El-Sayed setting single-day fundraising record
articles.summary: Abdul El-Sayed's campaign reports a $2.4 million single-day fundraising surge after Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers in Michigan.
articles.body: Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed’s campaign says it raised more than $2.4 million in a single day, setting a fundraising record in the final stretch of the Michigan race. The Democratic candidate's campaign said Sunday’s haul came from more than 65,000 donors, who gave an average of $36.74. Nearly 29,600 people contributed to the campaign for the first time. The fundraising surge came on the heels of Rep. Haley Stevens, D-Mich., endorsing Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers on Sunday after months of turmoil following her primary loss to the more progressive candidate. DEMOCRAT HALEY STEVENS ENDORSES GOP SENATE NOMINEE MIKE ROGERS "As Michiganders head to the polls, the momentum behind Abdul’s campaign has never been stronger," campaign spokesperson Cole Wozniak said in a statement following the final-hour cash haul. Stevens, who was considered the more moderate establishment candidate in her primary against El-Sayed earlier this year, said she remains "a very proud Democrat" who loves Michigan. She insisted, however, in the video message posted to social media over the weekend that she could not support El-Sayed, citing his backing from radical left-wing political streamer Hasan Piker. "Hey Michigan, as you may have seen, our Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Abdul said that I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away and he's right. And that's why I'm endorsing Mike Rogers for the United States Senate today," Stevens said in a video posted on X. The endorsement of the Trump-backed Republican candidate drew swift criticism from Democrats. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer called it "a despicable betrayal" and said his caucus in the upper chamber remains united behind El-Sayed. Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel also condemned Stevens’ decision, saying she had "abandoned everything she claims to care about." He also has attempted in recent months to distance himself from Piker amid the streamer's rising national recognition and increased scrutiny on his controversial statements — including antisemitic sentiments and claiming that "America deserved 9/11."

articles.title: Ex-FBI leader in Chicago sues DOJ, Blanche, Patel over ‘politically motivated’ Broadview Six case
articles.summary: Former Chicago FBI chief Douglas DePodesta sued President Trump and other top administration officials, alleging he was forced to resign after a federal prosecutor sought to blame him for the collapse of a controversial case against six protesters opposing the federal immigration crackdown. DePodesta, who led the FBI’s Chicago field office for nearly two years,…
articles.body:
Former Chicago FBI chief Douglas DePodesta sued President Trump and other top administration officials, alleging he was forced to resign after a federal prosecutor sought to blame him for the collapse of a controversial case against six protesters opposing the federal immigration crackdown.

DePodesta, who led the FBI’s Chicago field office for nearly two years, accused U.S. Attorney Andrew Boutros of orchestrating his removal after bringing “politically motivated prosecutions” that “were an unprecedented disaster” for his office to deflect scrutiny from the failed prosecution of the “Broadview Six,” according to the complaint filed in the Northern District of Illinois.

The lawsuit alleges that Boutros brought politically motivated charges against protesters during Operation Midway Blitz, the Trump administration’s sweeping immigration operation in the Chicago area last year.

After the case unraveled amid allegations of prosecutorial misconduct, the charges were dropped against the remaining defendants, as it was revealed that the grand jury was tainted during proceedings.

While several Illinois lawmakers called for Boutros’s resignation following the blowback, Boutros allegedly pressured senior Department of Justice (DOJ) officials in Washington to hold DePodesta responsible, ultimately leading to his ouster.

“I was forced to leave my job,” DePodesta told the Chicago Sun-Times in an interview published Monday. “I was ordered to leave my job.”

The lawsuit names Boutros, Attorney General Todd Blanche, FBI Director Kash Patel, the Justice Department and the FBI as defendants. DePodesta is seeking reinstatement, back pay, compensatory damages and attorney’s fees.

The legal challenge marks the latest fallout from the Broadview Six prosecution, which drew months of scrutiny over allegations of misconduct and political interference within the U.S. attorney’s office in Chicago.

The case stemmed from a Sept. 26, 2025, protest outside an Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) processing center in suburban Broadview, Ill., where more than 100 demonstrators gathered to oppose the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown.

Prosecutors accused six protesters of conspiring to impede a federal officer after a crowd allegedly surrounded and damaged an ICE officer’s vehicle.

Among those charged was former congressional candidate Kat Abughazaleh, who ran for a House seat in Illinois’s 9th Congressional District but lost the Democratic primary to former Evanston Mayor Daniel Biss.

articles.title: Trump, Hegseth underwater on approval from military members, veterans: Poll
articles.summary: President Trump and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth are underwater in their approval ratings with veterans and military members, according to a poll conducted by Common Defense. In a survey of 731 active-duty service members, veterans and military families, 67 percent of respondents said they believe military decisions under Trump are being made for political…
articles.body:
President Trump and Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth are underwater in their approval ratings with veterans and military members , according to a poll conducted by Common Defense.

In a survey of 731 active-duty service members, veterans and military families, 67 percent of respondents said they believe military decisions under Trump are being made for political gain. About 50 percent said they disapprove of Trump and Hegseth.

“Right now, nearly 8-in-10 veterans and military families say they’re being left behind, and active-duty troops are telling us that politicization is pushing them toward the exit. That’s not a talking point; it’s a readiness crisis,” said Jose Vasquez, U.S. Army veteran and executive director of Common Defense .

Fifty-three percent of respondents said they want to separate from the military sooner because of politicization, while 45 percent said policy changes or uncertainty under Trump made them want to exit sooner.

Still, 47 percent of respondents said the Republican Party does a better job at communicating with the military. The poll’s sample consisted of 47 percent Republicans and 35 percent Democrats.

Common Defense found 67 percent of respondents felt decisions that affect service members were being made for political gain and not mission readiness.

Hegseth has moved to reform the Pentagon through changes to readiness standards that often regard culture war issues and the implementation of a “warrior ethos.”

“Veterans know what real leadership looks like: you take care of the people under your command and you keep politics out of the mission,” Vasquez said.

Almost three-fourths of respondents expressed their disapproval of Congress. Forty-eight percent of active-duty respondents said they want the U.S. to pull out of Iran, while 55 percent want Congress to investigate the “deployments and troops’ health, safety, and welfare” during Operation Epic Fury in the Middle East.

Vasquez said military voters will consider candidates based on “what they’ve actually done for those who serve” and not on how emphatically they speak about supporting the military.

Common Defense reached respondents online and said the sample “skews older, whiter, more male, and more Republican.” The poll, taken in September and released in October, has a 4-point margin of error.

articles.title: Reflecting Pool dominates Trump’s closing midterm speech
articles.summary: President Trump’s closing speech a day before the midterm elections focused on the reopening of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and other changes around Washington, D.C. Trump in remarks at the Reflecting Pool announced its reopening. He showed pictures of what was replaced and said it should be a project that “unites all Americans.” “Today,…
articles.body:
President Trump’s closing speech a day before the midterm elections focused on the reopening of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and other changes around Washington, D.C.

Trump in remarks at the Reflecting Pool announced its reopening. He showed pictures of what was replaced and said it should be a project that “unites all Americans.”

“Today, I’m thrilled to announce the official opening of the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool,” he said.

He said they were considering renaming it the Trump Reflecting Pool but then said he was joking.

The pool has been fenced off for months after algae blooms and slits in the lining plagued the original renovation that Trump wanted.

The president didn’t touch on the midterm elections until roughly 20 minutes into his speech, focusing mostly on the pool repairs and other efforts to beautify D.C. , such as fixing fountains, removing graffiti and cutting down on crime.

“As you know, this is the last day before the midterm elections, the most important midterm I believe in our lifetime,” he said. “The Democrat Party has nominated the most extreme and dangerous slate of candidates in American history. These are the most dangerous candidates ever put up.”

He touted his administration’s achievements and hit on several candidates, such as Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, repeating claims about the nominee’s ties to the Muslim Brotherhood . Trump also touched on Alaska Senate candidate Dan J. Sullivan, who is running against incumbent GOP Sen. Dan S. Sullivan.

“We’ve achieved more in less than two years than any administration in American history, and I’ve kept every single promise I made, except far more,” he said. “I’ve actually kept far more promises than I made. We’ve done much more than I promised, and we have the most secure border in American history.”

He repeated his promise of giving American adults a $5,000 check if Republicans win the midterms.

He noted that he has traveled extensively the last few weeks to hold rallies, saying they were “full of love.”

“America is ready to go,” he said. “They’re ready to vote. I hope they’re ready to do the right thing.”

Trump said Republicans gave this election cycle “a very strong shot.”

“For some reason, the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms, but we gave this a very strong shot,” he said.

Trump spoke briefly about not allowing Iran to have a nuclear weapon before bringing his speech back to the Reflecting Pool.

articles.title: DOJ calls for sanctions over California voter rolls analysis
articles.summary: The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Sunday defended the accuracy of its claim that more than 20,000 “likely noncitizens” are on California’s voter rolls, even after an outside analysis found that more than 40 percent of the names flagged as noncitizens were not on the state’s voter rolls. DOJ officials wrote in a filing that…
articles.body:
The Department of Justice (DOJ) on Sunday defended the accuracy of its claim that more than 20,000 “likely noncitizens” are on California’s voter rolls, even after an outside analysis found that more than 40 percent of the names flagged as noncitizens were not on the state’s voter rolls.

DOJ officials wrote in a filing that the analysis made by the Coalition for Humane Immigrant Rights (CHIRLA) had nothing to do with the group’s legal standing, violating U.S. District Court Chief Judge James Boasberg’s order allowing them access to the federal government’s data on the 20,000 noncitizens.

The filing stated that Boasberg, an appointee of former President Obama, should hand the case to the department for investigation for possible criminal contempt of court.

“The report’s political grandstanding about alleged inaccuracies that purportedly impact California voters generally, or comparisons between the government’s list and the full ‘California voter file,’ has no relevance to whether the particular plaintiffs in this case have standing,” the filing stated.

Boasberg ordered CHIRLA not to disclose the names on the voter rolls and to use the data solely for their legal argument to challenge the Trump administration.

CHIRLA worked on the analysis with the University of California, Los Angeles’s Voting Rights Project, which filed the case. Voting Rights Project spokesperson Alberto Lammers told The Associated Press that the plaintiffs’ “counsel and their experts fully complied with the Court’s orders.”

On Monday, Boasberg allowed for a preliminary injunction blocking the DOJ from demanding California state officials segregate the noncitizens’ names from the voter rolls. He wrote that names on the lists were wrongly included and “that election officials’ ongoing review of those lists created a concrete risk to their ability to vote,” according to a statement from the Voting Rights Project.

“The court has seen the evidence and found that both our organization and our members are being harmed by this unconstitutional attack on the right to vote,” Angelica Salas, CHIRLA’s executive director, said in the Voting Rights Project’s statement .

“With Election Day tomorrow, this will give the needed breathing room to our citizen members and all other Californians who wish to vote, our volunteers and staff who engage in electoral work as well as to California officials who work so tirelessly to administer elections and protect the franchise,” Salas said.

The Trump administration brought its demand for California officials to separate the names of the alleged noncitizens to the Supreme Court on Monday. Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote to the high court that segregating the names from the rolls “is a routine remedy when the lawfulness of ballots is questioned.”

California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) said in a statement he had “strong reason” to believe his office would win against the administration again.

Doctors command the stage ahead of Election Day

Dozens of Democratic medical professionals are on the ballot for Congress and top state offices, a direct rebuke of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and the massive changes to federal health policy being made by the Trump administration.

Some of the most high-profile races tomorrow are focused on physicians, including Abdul El-Sayed for Senate in Michigan, Amy Acton for governor of Ohio, and Annie Andrews for Senate in South Carolina — a pediatrician who launched her campaign with an ad focused on getting kids vaccinated against measles.

If either El-Sayed or Andrews win their respective races, they would be the first Democratic M.D.s in the Senate since 1969 ; Andrews would be the first practicing Democratic physician in nearly 90 years.

There are roughly the same number of non-incumbent doctors and nurses running in this year’s election cycle as there currently are in Congress; seven physicians and 14 nurses compared to the 24 doctors and nurses currently in office.

According to Celinda Lake, a Democratic political strategist and president of Lake Research Partners, Kennedy’s Make American Healthy Again (MAHA) movement has spurred physicians to run for office.

“What MAHA has been good for is recruiting them, because so many of them see what’s going on and feel like they have to speak up. Because a lot of medical professionals have no desire to enter into politics, and this is a fairly new field for them. And I think what MAHA did was help energize them to run,” said Lake.

Health care is a major focus this election cycle, and numerous polls show Democrats have a significant trust advantage over Republicans.

“What I’ve heard from a lot of the doctors running is that they’ve come to the conclusion that there’s only so much they can accomplish from their exam rooms,” said Naughton. “And if they really want to make a difference at scale, this is the way to do it — is to take that very scary step to put your name out there and run for public office.”

articles.title: Forecasts of midterm blue wave put Trump’s legacy on line
articles.summary: President Trump’s political capital is on the line ahead of the midterm elections as a potential blue wave threatens his final two years in office. Trump has crisscrossed the country, holding 28 in-person campaign rallies in addition to a series of tele-rallies. The president has made stops in Republican strongholds like Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas…
articles.body:
President Trump’s political capital is on the line ahead of the midterm elections as a potential blue wave threatens his final two years in office.

Trump has crisscrossed the country, holding 28 in-person campaign rallies in addition to a series of tele-rallies. The president has made stops in Republican strongholds like Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas and even Alaska in an effort to keep the states firmly in the red column. He’s also visited a number of deep-red states like Mississippi and South Carolina, where polls show closer than expected races.

While Trump has argued his rallies have boosted Republican incumbents and candidates in the states, recent polling suggests otherwise.

A New York Times/Siena poll released the day before Election Day showed Democrats with leads in Senate races in Ohio, Texas, Iowa, Kansas and Alaska.

Trump’s heavy political investment in the states means he could end up shouldering the blame for a potential blue wave, which could impact the GOP beyond Election Day.

Republicans warn that a blue wave would be detrimental to the last two years of the Trump administration, and by extension, his legacy.

“It impacts his ability to drive policy over the next two years, or if a Supreme Court nomination comes up, or fill in the blank in terms of even Cabinet turnover,” said one Republican strategist, speaking on condition of anonymity. “All of that too will help shape his legacy, and it’s how people remember you at the end that guides you into the history books.”

In a statement to The Hill on Monday, the Republican National Committee (RNC) warned that Democrats would “obstruct” Trump’s agenda and that their “disastrous economic policies” would drive jobs overseas.

“The president knows what’s at stake this cycle, which is why he’s barnstormed the country to encourage our voters to support Republican candidates that will advance his agenda and deliver for the American people,” said RNC spokesperson Natalie Baldassarre.

But during an election eve speech at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, Trump did not appear entirely focused on the elections that could impact the trajectory of his last two years in office.

The president spent the first 22 minutes of his 37-minute address — largely viewed as a closing message before the midterms — talking about his administration’s efforts to repair the Reflecting Pool. Trump showed off a number of pre-renovation pictures of the pool and at one point invited Interior Secretary Doug Burgum to the podium to give brief remarks.

Trump also touted his numerous beautification projects and lower crime in the nation’s capital.

Republican operative Rob Stutzman called Trump’s speech “another Captain Queeg moment,” a reference to a character from Herman Wouk’s 1951 novel “The Caine Mutiny” who is considered an unstable and incompetent commander.

A second Republican strategist said, “What the utter f— was that?” when asked for their reaction to Trump’s speech at the Reflecting Pool.

“Republicans were hoping that he would have some sort of a closing message, some sort of American message with it, with a wonderful backdrop that could maybe be of help in the closing hours here,” the unnamed GOP strategist said. “As we Republicans are losing touch with the public, it looked like he was losing touch with reality.”

One national Republican operative noted the speech was “not surprising” considering Trump’s communication style but expressed frustration with the closing message.

“This perfectly encapsulates his messaging throughout this entire campaign cycle, but it’s deeply frustrating when we need to be laser-focused on turning out our low propensity voters tomorrow,” the operative said.

A third Republican strategist defended the speech, arguing the Reflecting Pool was “a hook” for Trump to be able to talk about issues like crime and immigration.

“It’s one of these things that wherever you get the opportunity to speak to a national audience, you’re going to talk about the midterms even if you have to start with something else,” the strategist said.

Trump did take some time during his speech Monday to urge Republicans to turn out on Election Day.

“If the people that voted for me and voted in the last election where we had such a great victory, if they go out and vote, just a good portion of them, we will win in a landslide,” the president said.

“Now, that doesn’t happen because usually whoever the sitting president is — Republican or Democrat, good or bad, good president, great president, bad president — for some reason the sitting president doesn’t win the midterms.”

“We gave this a very strong shot,” he added.

Much of the GOP’s strategy has hinged on turning out its low-propensity base as much as possible, arguably a tall order for any political party in a nonpresidential election. Republicans hoped to defy that trend by dispatching Trump on the campaign trail, urging voters to “pretend” like he is on the ballot.

“The amount of rallies he did shows he ‘believes’ that he’s on the ballot tomorrow,” said Dan Eberhart, a Republican donor. “He worked hard, and he’s right: Tomorrow’s outcome is a reflection on him.”

In a statement to The Hill, White House spokesperson Davis Ingle referred to Trump as the GOP’s “best messenger” and “unmatched motivator” who is “committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress.”

But some Republicans are unsure whether that tactic will ultimately work.

“So far from what we’ve seen, those rallies have not done what they were meant to do,” said the first unnamed Republican strategist.

Democrats have been heartened by signs of early turnout in key battlegrounds, but Republicans argue that a large share of their voters tend to vote in person on Election Day.

“They’re banking on these Republicans and the folks that he’s trying to rally to show up tomorrow, and Republicans historically and should do exceedingly well tomorrow,” the first Republican strategist said. “But the fact is, they still underperformed in places like Texas and in Florida in the early vote.”

According to data released by Texas’s secretary of State, 7.7 million voters in the Lone Star State voted early.

Meanwhile in Florida, registered Republicans led registered Democrats in early voting by just a little more than 200,000 voters. By comparison, in 2022, registered Republicans led Democrats in early voting by just a little less than 500,000 voters.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis (R) on Sunday sounded the alarm over low turnout in the state, which has become known as a nerve center for Republican politics.

“If people stay home, you could end up seeing results that you’re going to be wondering what happened. That’s just the reality,” DeSantis said at a campaign event.

“The reality is gas is higher, and that’s not good. Some of these Republicans act like it’s no big deal. I disagree with that. It is a big deal to people,” the Florida governor continued.

articles.summary: Thousands of voters in Washoe County, Nev., received mail-in ballot return envelopes with the word “FALSE” written on them. A spokesperson for the county’s Registrar of Voters, George Guthrie, said in a statement to The Hill that the affected envelopes were “not limited to voters of any particular political party.” “The inclusion of the word…
articles.body:
Thousands of voters in Washoe County, Nev., received mail-in ballot return envelopes with the word “FALSE” written on them.

A spokesperson for the county’s Registrar of Voters, George Guthrie, said in a statement to The Hill that the affected envelopes were “not limited to voters of any particular political party.”

“The inclusion of the word ‘FALSE’ on mail ballot return envelopes resulted from a printing error that affected approximately 32,000 envelopes in the initial production batch prepared by our ballot printing vendor,” Guthrie continued.

Envelopes intended to indicate which voters required additional identification under state law were meant to display “TRUE” in a hidden “ID Required” field, according to Guthrie, though “for voters not requiring additional identification, no designation was intended to appear, but the printing error caused ‘FALSE’ to be printed on their envelopes.”

“The error was promptly identified and corrected in subsequent batches and did not affect voter registration records, identification requirements, the validity of the ballots or voters’ ability to cast their ballots,” he concluded.

Nevada is one state where Democrats are looking to expand, particularly in the state’s gubernatorial race. Nevada Gov. Joe Lombardo (R) is running to defend his seat from opponent state Attorney General Aaron Ford (D).

The race is designated as a toss-up by Cook Political Report , which noted in its analysis that “things looked better earlier this year” for Lombardo “before the reality of the national environment fully set in.”

President Trump won the state by about 3 points in 2024, but Lombardo has struggled to build a similar lead against his opponent in polls leading up to Election Day.

Ford’s campaign has picked up steam following a rally with former Vice President Kamala Harris in late October and an appearance at a candidate debate that Lombardo declined to participate in.

Nevada Secretary of State Francisco Aguilar (D) told The Hill that “vendors working in the election space need to hold themselves to the highest standard and be aware that their actions can have a significant impact on voter confidence.”

“Nevadans deserve better and the Secretary of State’s Office is evaluating our options for future elections,” Aguilar continued.

articles.title: Supreme Court rejects Trump administration’s bid to set aside 20,000 California ballots
articles.summary: The Supreme Court on Monday quickly rejected the Trump administration’s effort to force California officials to set aside 20,000 ballots it claims belong to likely noncitizens and must be investigated. The court’s one-sentence order contained no explanation and had no noted dissents. California and immigration rights groups question the veracity of the administration’s list and…
articles.body:
The Supreme Court on Monday quickly rejected the Trump administration’s effort to force California officials to set aside 20,000 ballots it claims belong to likely noncitizens and must be investigated.

The court’s one-sentence order contained no explanation and had no noted dissents.

California and immigration rights groups question the veracity of the administration’s list and say its lawsuit is an attempt to disenfranchise legal voters. The administration raced its claims to the Supreme Court earlier on Monday after California persuaded lower courts that the administration has no legal right to push the state to comply.

It’s one of multiple legal cases the Justice Department (DOJ) has launched in the final weeks leading up to the midterm contests. The DOJ has also emerged unsuccessful in Alaska, as it looks to block certification of the state’s Senate race over a second candidate with the same name as the incumbent.

Although it technically is not the end of the lawsuit in California, the Supreme Court’s emergency ruling appears to mark the final word ahead of Election Day.

All sides agree that ballots can’t be separated once they’re processed, and election officials have already received hundreds of thousands of mail ballots ahead of polls opening on Tuesday. It left the administration warning the justices that the clock was running out.

“The only way to preserve the district court’s ability to grant relief to the United States after a full merits proceeding, therefore, is to segregate the challenged ballots now. That remedy would not cause any undue hardship to California,” Solicitor General D. John Sauer wrote to the court.

The court rejected the bid within hours and without ordering California to file a response.

The Trump administration launched its lawsuit against California last month as it alleged the state was sending 20,000 likely noncitizens ballots as part of its universal mail-in voting program. All active, registered California voters are automatically sent a ballot. U.S. District Judge David Carter, an appointee of former President Clinton assigned the case, ruled last week that California could continue to accept the questioned ballots like any other.

“This request violates longstanding constitutional principles mandating that states have control over their elections,” Carter wrote. “If Plaintiff’s last-minute request for relief were granted, either party could create chaos for their own political purposes to disrupt the election process,” he continued. “Over 20,000 registered Californians would potentially lose the right that generations of Americans have fought to preserve.”

The Trump administration asked the Supreme Court to intervene after an appeals court declined to intervene in a 2-1 vote on Friday .

Ahead of the Supreme Court’s decision, California Attorney General Rob Bonta (D) said the appeal “reeks of desperation” and called it an attempt to undermine Tuesday’s election.

“My message to Californians is simple: Election Day is tomorrow, but don’t wait until then to vote. If you haven’t cast your ballot yet, make a plan to do so as soon as possible. We’ll keep handling the legal fight in court,” Bonta said in a statement.

The Hill has reached out to Bonta’s office and the Justice Department for comment.

articles.title: How National Guard units are being deployed around the midterm elections
articles.summary: National Guard members in at least seven states will have some form of a role around Tuesday’s highly charged midterm elections. As Americans head to the polls, plain clothes National Guard soldiers are set to help monitor ballot boxes in seven Washington state counties, Iowa guardsmen are tasked with monitoring and defending election networks, and…
articles.body:
National Guard members in at least seven states will have some form of a role around Tuesday’s highly charged midterm elections.

As Americans head to the polls, plain clothes National Guard soldiers are set to help monitor ballot boxes in seven Washington state counties, Iowa guardsmen are tasked with monitoring and defending election networks, and Colorado Guard members will be assisting with election cybersecurity.

Those are just a few examples of the military’s role before and during Nov. 3, an election that has received intense scrutiny as Democrats look to win control of the House and Senate and President Trump has asserted he would do “anything necessary” to ensure honest elections.

A majority of Americans, however, do not think troops should be used at polling sites.

A new survey released by The Democracy and Security Network at the German Marshall Fund of the United States said those pushing back at the use of troops at the polls say it damages the public’s confidence in the military as an institution.

Loren Voss, one of the researchers who conducted the survey, said that out of the 2,800 Americans polled, 59 percent said that the president should not use the federal military to monitor or administer elections.

She told The Hill there is a generalized fear around federal interference in the elections, be it by a federalized National Guard presence, or Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), or FBI agents, and having members of the military help around polling stations only adds to that concern of interference.

“This is just another instance of using the National Guard for something that should be a civilian mission,” she said on the use of the guard at ballot boxes in Washington. “That is just so fraught for the potential of people thinking that there’s something untoward going on. You just shouldn’t take that risk.”

Federal law generally does not allow armed personnel to be stationed at a place where an election is being held – with the exception being a polling location is being attacked where federal force is needed.

But in the past several presidential and midterm elections, state governors have increasingly called on their National Guard to monitor cybersecurity and assist local authorities. In 2022 at least 14 states used their guardsmen, a number that rose to 15 in 2024.

This year, seven states have publicly acknowledged the Guard’s involvement in the midterms, with Washington drawing the most attention after Gov. Bob Ferguson (D) last month offered counties an “Election Neighborhood Watch.” Seven counties took Ferguson up on his offer; the mobilization will consist of about 100 total National Guard troops.

Speaking to reporters on Friday, Ferguson pointed to the 2024 incident when an unknown arsonist threw an incendiary device into a ballot box in Vancouver, Wash., damaging several hundred ballots. Then-Gov. Jay Inslee activated the National Guard to assist after the event.

Ferguson also referred to recent reports of letters containing white powder sent to the secretary of state’s office and to several congressional offices.

“[We want to] just take every precaution we can to make sure that we’re protecting our voting system,” he said. “The National Guard, just so we’re clear, is called up routinely for elections, for cybersecurity and other things.”

In North Carolina, the National Guard’s Joint Cyber Security Task Force will help monitor election networks, along with the state’s Emergency Operations Center, a guard official told The Hill. They added that their Civil Support Teams are always on standby but they have not been alerted at this time.

Colorado Governor Jared Polis (D) in June ordered his National Guard to assist with election cybersecurity, the only election support that the Secretary of State’s Office has requested at this time, The Hill was told.

Iowa guardsmen, meanwhile, would work alongside Iowa Secretary of State Paul Pate and state partners with its “specialized cybersecurity expertise, technical capabilities and operational experience to help identify potential cyber threats, strengthen defensive readiness and improve coordination among state agencies,” Brig. Gen. Mark Kappelman announced last week.

The Alabama and Oklahoma National Guards already have been used after their specialists in October responded to two separate incidents where suspicious packages containing white powder were mailed to the Alabama Secretary of State’s office and the Oklahoma State Election Board.

Arizona also will reportedly have its guard assist in the midterms but its office did not respond to questions from The Hill as to what they would look like.

Elsewhere, Democratic lawmakers have expressed concerns that the Trump administration may use the military or ICE agents to intimidate voters or election workers, contest the results of certain races, or seize voting machines or ballots. Trump in an January interview with The New York Times said that he regretted not ordering the National Guard to seize voting machines in swing states after he lost the 2020 election.

Officials with the Department of Homeland Security have said they do not plan to send ICE officers to patrol polls.

In Washington, D.C., meanwhile, the National Guard has been deployed by Trump since last year and will be on patrol on election day, though the city has asked the guard to limit the placement of troops near mail ballot drop boxes.

Senate Armed Services Committee member Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.), earlier this fall sent letters to Attorney General Todd Blanche, Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin, FBI Director Kash Patel and Chief of the National Guard General Steven Nordhaus asking for a commitment to keep federal forces and law enforcement agents out of the midterm elections.

Joint Chiefs of Staff Chair Gen. Dan Caine earlier in August assured Slotkin in letter that there were no plans to send troops to seize election-related materials.

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth in a Sept. 22 directive, however, ordered military spy agencies to “mobilize every asset . . . to defend our election” so that “every lawful voter can cast their ballot free from foreign intimidation, coercion, or fear.”

Trump also has refused to rule out invoking the Insurrection Act or declaring a national emergency around the midterm elections.

articles.summary: {beacon} Energy & Environment Energy & Environment The Big Story Oil prices fall ahead of midterms President Trump on Monday touted a new drop in oil prices during his closing pitch to voters ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections. © Alex Brandon, Associated Press International benchmark Brent crude was trading at $104 Monday afternoon, down…
articles.body:
President Trump on Monday touted a new drop in oil prices during his closing pitch to voters ahead of Tuesday’s midterm elections.

International benchmark Brent crude was trading at $104 Monday afternoon, down from $112 earlier in the day. U.S. benchmark WTI was trading at about $96 per barrel, down from nearly $103.

The price drop came amid some signs of positivity in talks with Iran. Tehran offered to reopen the Strait of Hormuz if the U.S. agreed to meet certain conditions, but it is unclear if the U.S. will meet those conditions. There has also been talk in Washington of new strikes on Iran after the midterm elections.

The war has periodically seen closures of the Strait of Hormuz, a key oil shipping lane, as well as higher costs to transport oil even when ships have been allowed to pass through. Damage to oil infrastructure in that conflict and the Russia-Ukraine conflict have also put upward pressure on prices.

“Oil today is down $10,” Trump said Monday while delivering his closing midterm remarks at the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington.

“It’s going to go down a lot further because we’re winning with Iran, easily winning,” he added.

Trump claimed that the decline was “the biggest drop in oil in history.”

Recent history has seen larger drops; during the COVID-19 pandemic, oil prices on one day briefly sank to about negative $38 per barrel, falling by far more than $10.

Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) on Monday went after former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), who is running for Senate in Michigan, over his claims that more young people are “against the Jews.”

In an appearance on CBS News’s “60 Minutes” broadcast Sunday , Rogers said that “the next generation of kids thinks it’s really cool to be against the Jews.”

“What are we doing? This sounds like 1933. It doesn’t sound like today, and that’s not the America I wore the uniform to defend, and that’s not the America I want to live in. So, we’re going to have to have conversations, and some of them are going to be really hard,” he added.

Massie shot back at Rogers over his comments in a post on the social platform X Monday.

“This is false and dangerous rhetoric from Mike Rogers: ‘The next generation of kids thinks it’s really cool to be against the Jews,’” Massie said in his post. “No Mike, the next generation and my generation and the generations in between are against funding wars in the Middle East.”

“Mike and others do a great disservice to Jewish people when they imply that opposition to Netanyahu’s wars is equivalent to antisemitism,” he added.

Massie has led a push in Congress to cut off U.S. aid to Israel, an issue that has gained steam amid Israel’s war in Gaza.

A growing cohort of Democrats have labeled Israel’s actions in that war, in which tens of thousands of Palestinians have been killed, as “genocide” — including Rogers’s Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed.

Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.), who lost to El-Sayed in the primary, cited the Democrats’ positions on Israel in her decision to endorse Rogers over the weekend.

Earlier this year, House Democrats split almost evenly on an amendment to stop U.S. aid to Israel, signaling how far the party has shifted on the relationship. Massie spearheaded that amendment, which failed in a 104-314 vote, with Massie as the lone Republican yes vote.

Netanyahu is currently locked in a fight for his political survival after Israeli elections last month. While Netanyahu’s coalition received the most votes, he came up short of a clear majority, meaning his leading opponent, Gadi Eisenkot, may have the first chance to form a government.

articles.body:
Chaos in Michigan is raising the stakes even higher in one of the most closely watched Senate battles in the nation.

The political world was agog on Sunday when Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) endorsed the GOP’s Senate candidate, former Rep. Mike Rogers (R-Mich.), over her party colleague Abdul El-Sayed.

Democrats immediately and fiercely denounced Stevens, and several senior lawmakers made it known she had promised them she would make no such endorsement of Rogers — right before doing so.

The Michigan Senate race was always compelling.

On one side, El-Sayed is seeking to become the first Muslim senator in the nation’s history, having vanquished Stevens in a bitter primary that divided in large part over views of Israel.

On the other, Rogers is seeking to hold back the anti-Republican tide that appears to be rising elsewhere in the nation. President Trump has sought to buoy Rogers but has done so through Islamophobic attacks on El-Sayed, whom he has repeatedly called a “jihadist.”

During weekend rallies, Trump said the Senate would have “to get a special metal detector for Abdul” if El-Sayed were elected. A previous use of that attack line had prompted El-Sayed to respond , “I’ll go through a metal detector every day. You sit through a lie detector one time. That’s the deal.”

Stevens’s shock decision to endorse Rogers, however, also threatens to play into tensions between the left and the centrists in the Democratic Party that have risen sharply in recent months.

Although El-Sayed does not identify as a socialist and is not a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), he is plainly identified with the left of the party. Pledges to back Medicare-for-All and to rid politics of big-money influences are a central part of his platform.

The available evidence suggests El-Sayed could prevail, regardless of Stevens’s late backing of his opponent.

The El-Sayed campaign said it raised $1.2 million in just four hours after the congresswoman’s endorsement of Rogers. The bizarreness of Stevens’s move — and the strange interviews she gave to justify it, most notably to CNN’s Anderson Cooper on Sunday evening — appear to have caused Democrats to coalesce behind El-Sayed even more strongly. And the final spate of polls from the highly-regarded New York Times/Siena College partnership put El-Sayed up by 11 points.

An 11-point victory for El-Sayed in a state Trump won, albeit very narrowly, two years ago would be a startling result. Even some supporters of the candidate don’t expect him to prevail by that much. And those same supporters also have keen memories of how the polls in the primary were way off, predicting El-Sayed would defeat Stevens by double-digits, when he actually won by a single point.

If El-Sayed were to lose, internal party mayhem is guaranteed. Social media voices on the left excoriated Stevens for her endorsement of Rogers over the weekend — and so too did some centrist figures.

Former Clinton strategist James Carville took to YouTube to insist that Stevens’s “political career is over” — a common view in Democratic circles — and suggest she had not got a high enough price “if you’re going to sell your soul.”

CNN commentator Van Jones, another centrist figure who often draws criticism from the left, said on the network that “Haley just flushed herself down the toilet.”

Meanwhile, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-N.Y.) told Politico that Stevens had made a “terrible decision” and that the party would consider “appropriate next steps” regarding her conduct when Congress returns.

Some on the left, appalled as they are by Stevens’s decisions, are reluctant to see her move as emblematic of the broader struggle between the Democratic Party’s left flank and its more centrist establishment, however.

“I think this is a one-off,” progressive strategist and organizer Jonathan Tasini told this column. “I don’t think you can draw a line from her behavior to the bigger picture of the Democratic Party.”

Be that as it may, the tensions between the left and the center could easily ramp up after the election.

Beside El-Sayed’s electoral fate, a number of other candidates from the harder edges of the left are almost sure to be elected.

Two DSA members, Darializa Avila Chevalier and Claire Valdez, are likely to win House races in New York. Chevalier defeated a Democratic incumbent in her primary, as did another New York progressive who is all but sure to be on his way to Congress after Tuesday, Brad Lander.

In Colorado’s 1st District, DSA member Melat Kiros (D) is again a near-certainty to win, having dispatched Rep. Diana DeGette in the primary. DeGette had first been elected to the House in 1996, the year before Kiros was born.

The new crop of left-leaning figures will join the original members of the so-called “Squad,” all of whom are overwhelming favorites to win reelection: Reps. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), Ilhan Omar (D-Minn.), Ayanna Pressley (D-Mass.) and Rashida Tlaib (D-Mich.). Speculation is rampant that Ocasio-Cortez could run for president — or primary Senate Minority Leader Charles Schumer (D-N.Y.) — in 2028.

Despite all that, centrist figures argue that the party should not take what they see as the wrong lessons if Democrats have a strong night on Tuesday.

“Are you trying to make blue places bluer, or are you trying to turn red and purple places blue?” Jim Kessler, executive vice president at the centrist Third Way asked rhetorically. “For Democrats, we need to win majorities.”

Kessler argued that the real story of this midterm cycle so far was how moderate Democratic candidates have put states that are usually seen as reliably Republican, or at least GOP-leaning, in play. He alluded to Senate candidates such as James Talarico in Texas, Adam Hamilton in Kansas and Josh Turek in Iowa.

“If the polls are anywhere near accurate, centrist Democrats are about to rewrite the Senate and electoral college map,” Kessler added. “We are going to be winning places that were pipe dreams for Democrats for 20, 30, or in some cases the last one hundred years. Centrist Democrats are expanding the map.”

Even Tasini, who spoke to this column briefly on his way to do door-to-door canvassing in Portland, Ore., argued that the left should not get too carried away even if its candidates do well, noting that the majority of Democrats in federal office remain centrist in orientation.

“We will have a bigger megaphone,” he said of the left. “There will be more members who can hold forth on the House and Senate floor about these issues. But I don’t think we’ll have hit nirvana, or that in two years we are going to transform the country.”

Others on the left may be less patient, however — and that could spell new clashes to come.

The Memo is a reported column by Niall Stanage .

articles.body:
Sen. Tammy Duckworth (D-Ill.) condemned President Trump’s recent low flyover on Halloween in a Monday letter to Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) Administrator Bryan Bedford, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Director Russell Vought.

The flyover occurred last Thursday during the White House’s Halloween party with Air Force One making two low altitude passes around the South Lawn.

An FAA official said the flights were coordinated with the agency.

Duckworth — ranking member of the Subcommittee on Aviation, Space and Innovation — described how the passes by Air Force One “startled residents, prompted 911 calls and forced a ground stop at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport (DCA),” which resulted in more than 200 flight delays.

“For the children on the [South Lawn], perhaps a treat; for everyone else in the National Capital Region (NCR) and across the country, a trick—dangerous, expensive and profoundly unserious,” she wrote.

The Council of D.C. office’s X account confirmed “anyone in downtown DC, at the Pentagon or at National Airport” had been given 15 minutes notice before the flight.

“Residents who lived through September 11, 2001, when a hijacked airliner struck the Pentagon, dialed 911 fearing an attack,” Duckworth continued. “The White House insisted the flyover ‘brought joy and excitement.’ Tell that to the people who called 911.”

She is questioning Bedford, Hegseth and Vought on the approval process taken before the flyover and if proper notification procedures had been followed. She also asked they provide “a complete accounting of the cost to taxpayers.”

“As with all congressional correspondence, the Department will respond directly to the authors,” a Defense Department official told The Hill.

“The country got a trick dressed up as a treat—and another reminder that this unserious President is more interested in impressing children with his toys than in meeting the needs of the American people,” Duckworth concluded.

The flyovers also come after the 2025 midair collision over the Potomac River, near DCA. An Army Black Hawk helicopter collided with an American Airlines flight when it was seconds away from landing at National Airport. None of the people on board either aircraft survived.

A U.S. army report noted the “most salient contributing factor” was two broken radio transmissions, which resulted in the Army UH-60 Black Hawk helicopter, or PAT 25, not receiving “critical details” from DCA’s air traffic control tower.

OMB did not respond immediately to The Hill’s request for comment.
